docs.title: Agentmux
docs.text: Run coding agents together, control what they share, and inspect checked changes before applying them to your project.

docs.title: Start with your native subscriptions
docs.text:
Install Agentmux and sign in to Claude Code and Codex. From your project, start a workspace and review task pairing:

amx start --detach
amx pair claude codex --delivery auto

Pairing previews the mutual command grants, both delivery modes, returned results and existing queues. Add --apply after reviewing it, then amx attach claude. Auto can start eligible existing work and future work from all permitted senders; choose --delivery review for exact item approval. Task pairing and installed-provider selection require v0.15.0 or later. The short quickstart covers ordinary setup.

For a checked coding request in a separate worktree, preview amx work "Change" -- CHECK. To inspect the mechanics without provider setup, run amx demo; it changes only its own disposable Git fixture. See your first checked result.

docs.title: Choose your starting point
docs.text:
Goal Guide Execution starts when Inspect a checked fixture without configuring providers Your first checked result Run amx demo; it changes only its generated repository Ask for one checked coding change Work on a task Add --allow-models after inspecting the preview Type directly in several native conversations Short native quickstart Start a workspace and use its native terminals Inspect reporting, pending work or uncertain delivery Observability Inspection starts no execution; choose the workspace explicitly Compare alternatives, build a mission or review changed snapshots Advanced workflows Run an owner-authored plan; provider turns require --allow-models Queue tasks or enable bounded autonomous teams Managed setup Launch a reviewed team configuration Run controlled cooperation or competition studies Research Run a declared study; model participants require explicit opt-in

The visual guide illustrates the coding journey and the native terminal/web controls. Work sessions covers session discovery, workspace switching and individual-session recovery. A source build remains an alternative to release binaries.

v0.15.0 includes the daily power-user controls: amx context explains the selected workspace, amx tasks searches retained delegation history, and amx task ID --open -s NAME opens the exact task's evidence and recovery controls. amx observe summarizes fresh broker/worker reporting and complete retained task counts, with bounded attention and optional JSONL watching. Both terminal and web Actions offer Tasks for selected session. Upgrade existing workspace controllers explicitly; see everyday commands for the five daily loops.

Keep the everyday command reference handy for selecting named workspaces, adding or connecting sessions, and choosing a collaboration group's board. For a repeated-round study, start with the research planning and observation workflow.

The managed runtime and workbench are experimental. Broker permissions, native approvals, provider networking and filesystem isolation are separate boundaries. The trust model and validation guide describe enforced boundaries, reproducible checks and limits.

docs.text: Quality and evidence describes what the checks establish and what remains unproven. Use matched workflow evaluations to measure task quality, time and cost. Release validation covers installable artifacts and release checks.

docs.title: Existing workspace mode
docs.text:
The original YAML compiler creates tmux layouts with load and reload. Pane capture, raw input, synchronization, session KV and portable bundles remain available. This mode does not provide the managed broker's per-agent ACLs.

Workspace quickstart · Layout architecture · Portable bundles

docs.title: Antigravity inference with isolated Pi agents
docs.text:
For an ordinary local Antigravity terminal in an already-running workspace:

amx add --session work --harness antigravity --native-only \
  --project . --title "Antigravity investigation"

This uses its normal native configuration with no Agentmux prompt injection. Use its stable ID to attach or configure manual coordination; native tools and history stay in that terminal. There is no verified native appended-system-role flag. The bridge below is the separate option for injected Agentmux context, isolated Pi tools and managed persistent turns. See work sessions and provider compatibility for setup and verification steps.

Antigravity's native CLI supports trusted-local fresh managed turns. Its native keyring and private history layout are not a verified independent sandbox contract. The optional inference bridge keeps that native login in an owner-controlled host service, while Pi provides each agent's isolated tools and private persistent conversation. No host home, keyring, DBus socket, or native Antigravity history is mounted into an agent.

Start an authenticated loopback bridge and keep its key in the controller's environment. Generate a new private key rather than copying this example text:

export AGENTMUX_AGY_BRIDGE_KEY="$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))')"
amx provider antigravity serve \
  --listen 127.0.0.1:8097 \
  --models gemini-3.8-flash-low \
  --max-concurrent 1 --max-requests 20 --timeout 45s &
bridge_pid=$!

This uses the explicitly selected host agy executable and its existing login; it does not log in or change provider settings. Native CLI processes run in a fresh empty private working directory. Every invocation applies deny rules for all documented native file, command, URL, unsandboxed-command, and MCP action namespaces through --settings. Native tool events fail the request. The service is trusted host code and consumes the owner's native CLI configuration; only use it with a reviewed native installation/configuration. Native provider history/logging can retain inference prompts on the host, outside agent access.

Set up the isolated client from the same shell, preserving the bridge key:

amx managed setup --spec examples/managed/setup-antigravity-bridge.json --output agy-team.yaml
amx managed up agy-team.yaml --broker-sandbox bubblewrap
# When the managed run is finished:
amx managed down --state /absolute/path/to/its/state
kill "$bridge_pid"
wait "$bridge_pid"
unset AGENTMUX_AGY_BRIDGE_KEY

The setup harness alias antigravity-bridge produces a pi agent connected to the supplied bridge API. Its authenticated HTTP key is an inference capability, not the underlying Google/OAuth credential. The example uses a network namespace with an exact-origin allowlist and an explicit loopback IP pin. Pi receives only its private broker credential, selected bridge key, explicit code dependencies, workspace and session generation. The provider service needs a separate lifecycle from the managed team; starting/stopping a team does not silently start a credential-bearing service.

The service exposes authenticated /v1/models and /v1/chat/completions only. It rejects non-loopback binds, browser-origin requests, unlisted models, unsupported roles, excessive bodies, schemas, output and concurrency. The default allowance is 100 native requests, not a billing guarantee. A request deadline is at most two minutes. Native failures consume an accepted allowance and are not retried by the bridge. A calling harness can have its own HTTP retry behavior; the finite service allowance still bounds native requests. Output token requests are advisory to native Antigravity; the enforced bridge bound is 128 KiB of response text plus the process deadline. No hard provider token or currency ceiling is claimed.

Client tools are translated to a strict textual JSON response contract. The bridge validates the returned function name and arguments against the exact declared schema and translates them to OpenAI tool-call messages. It never executes these tools. Pi executes the resulting calls inside its own sandbox. Supported schemas cover bounded object/array/primitive types, required fields, additional properties, enums/constants, unions, numeric/string/collection bounds and RE2-compatible patterns. Unsupported schemas/forced tool choices fail closed. This is a compatibility layer, not native OpenAI tool calling, native Antigravity session resume, vision, realtime streaming, or a claim that all OpenAI API features are implemented. SSE begins after the native turn completes.

docs.title: Verify your installation
docs.text:
These opt-in checks separate isolated tool execution with a fake native process from two real inference turns. The live check requires an existing native login and consumes provider requests:

# No provider calls: real Pi/Bubblewrap + fake native process
AGENTMUX_PI_SANDBOX_LIVE=1 go test -race -v ./internal/agybridge -run TestPiSandboxBridge
# Makes at most TWO native Flash calls; requires an existing local agy login
AGENTMUX_AGY_PI_LIVE=1 go test -race -v ./internal/agybridge -run TestAntigravityBridgeRealPiPersistentTwoTurns

The native behavior follows the official headless protocol, permission rules, and per-session settings.

docs.title: Persistent conversations and bounded autonomous workflows
docs.text:
Managed workers can run several turns from one initial goal. Three controls are independent: the native harness conversation, broker command authority, and the events that may wake a worker. Configure each agent explicitly.

agents:
  lead:
    harness: claude
    sandbox: bubblewrap
    network: host
    conversation: persistent
    autonomy:
      enabled: true
      boards: [work]
      direct_notes: false
      pings: true
      max_turns: 20
      cooldown_seconds: 2
      max_backlog: 50
      batch_size: 10
      max_hops: 8

This fragment belongs in a version 2 managed configuration, alongside role, authentication, board access, instruction grants and resource limits. Enabling a subscription does not grant access to its board or permission to command anyone. Defaults preserve fresh turns and no message-triggered execution. See the autonomy operation reference for exact defaults, queue receipts, omitted-source references and causal ancestry bounds.

docs.title: Native history
docs.text:
conversation: persistent uses an explicit native session reference for Claude, Codex or Pi inside Bubblewrap. Each agent and conversation generation receives its own writable transcript directory. Credentials are separate filtered, read-only snapshots. Peer histories and the controller state directory are not mounted. Antigravity and the generic command harness reject persistent mode; their managed turns remain explicitly fresh.

This managed-history contract is separate from interactive native sessions. Those keep their normal provider terminal/history and can be deliberately relaunched with an explicit native history choice after exit. No managed conversation reference is guessed from a native task title.

The worker reintroduces the role, current task and authenticated provenance on every turn. Previous conversation text does not create broker permissions. Only a confirmed successful native turn and atomic task completion commit a session reference. There is no implicit “last session,” fallback to a fresh conversation, or replay after an uncertain response.

Inspect a reference using the owner credential:

amx managed call conversation.status --credential-file STATE/owner.json \
  --json '{"agent":"lead"}'

An interrupted, cancelled or failed persistent turn blocks history reuse. First stop its process and resolve any uncertain task using the managed task recovery procedure. Then explicitly start a new conversation generation:

amx managed call conversation.reset --credential-file STATE/owner.json \
  --json '{"agent":"lead"}'

Reset preserves old transcripts for owner inspection. It does not renew the session deadline or autonomy budget. Native transcript retention consumes disk; archive completed state directories according to your retention policy. Native history is a resume mechanism, not an immutable full tool audit.

docs.title: Observations and commands
docs.text:
An authorized instruct creates an instruction task. A subscribed board post, direct note or ping can instead create an observation task. Its provenance lists the triggering message references; its text does not impersonate a human or a commanding agent. The worker resolves those references through wake.read under current access and team-history rules immediately before execution.

The broker keeps a durable bounded unread queue, batches triggers, suppresses self-authored wakeups and carries causal ancestry. It enforces a finite causal hop limit. Overflow retains the original message but drops the extra wake notification and increments a visible counter. Agents can still read messages through normal authorized operations. A wakeup is not a guarantee of eventual execution after budget exhaustion, revocation or expiry.

With autonomy enabled, owner and peer instructions also consume the same per-agent turn budget. Cooldowns and serial execution apply to every launch. Budgets, unread state and owner pause state survive broker restarts. Workers check readiness without writing idle polling receipts. Unknown or interrupted deliveries retain their slots until explicitly resolved.

Use autonomy.status {"agent":"lead"} with the owner credential (or {} with the agent's credential). autonomy.control is owner-only and accepts the agent, latest status version, and mode running, paused or stopped. Pausing prevents further launches; cancellation of already running work uses task.cancel and its process-stopped acknowledgement. Do not infer that a pause has stopped an in-flight native tool. There is no automatic budget renewal.

Read-only capacity.get exposes remaining lifetime allocations, delegated templates, admission state and reasons. Owner capacity.update can explicitly change future token/cost admission allowances or shorten admission runtime with a resource version; it does not replenish lifetime autonomy turns or extend the process deadline. Live permissions describes that separate control. Role edits are also explicit owner CAS operations: managed workers capture the current role at their next task claim; an active native terminal receives a broker notice instead of injected input.

docs.title: Reproduce a bounded workflow
docs.text:
python3 scripts/smoke-managed-autonomy.py --binary bin/amx --allow-models runs a bounded five-turn Claude/Codex workflow. It requires installed authenticated CLIs, working Bubblewrap, and user-systemd cgroup enforcement. It makes up to five real cloud turns; model calls are never automatically retried. All agents and the broker use separate namespaces. Scoped artifacts pass through broker memory, the coder can ping but cannot command the lead, and an independent credential-free verifier checks the final artifact before owner verification.

The fixture restarts the broker between confirmed turns, preserves its pending wakeup, resumes both native histories, and requires exactly one initial owner instruction. Private artifacts and a secret-safe JSON report distinguish a verified run from a failed or uncertain attempt. Scripted broker and native protocol tests cover failure, revocation, budget and replay cases without cloud calls.

Both live acceptance runners first check the independent verifier against known passing and failing implementations, without model calls. Verifier diagnostics (command, exit status and bounded output) are retained privately beside each artifact; a final verifier failure is also recorded in report.json. The verifier uses a system Python under /usr, so a host virtualenv or PATH shim outside its mounts cannot accidentally become its interpreter.

To recheck a retained implementation without restarting agents or spending more model turns:

python3 scripts/smoke-managed-models.py \
  --verify-artifact /path/to/retained/tag_normalizer.py

This produces a separate artifact-only report and private diagnostics. It does not change the original run's status or verify its broker tasks. A standalone verifier preflight is also available:

python3 scripts/smoke-managed-models.py --check-fixtures

docs.title: Message wakeups and bounded agent turns
docs.text:
Autonomy is opt-in per agent. It lets an idle worker react to selected observations while keeping instruct as a separately authorized command. Subscriptions grant no board access, team membership, or instruction authority.

These controls dispatch managed task workers. Interactive native sessions use the separate native delivery policy: Manual by default, with explicit Review/Auto and observation subscriptions. They retain their ordinary terminal workflow. Use work sessions for that daily interactive setup and autonomous workflows for persistent managed turns.

agents:
  reviewer:
    harness: codex
    role: Review supplied changes; wait when there is nothing useful to do.
    autonomy:
      enabled: true
      boards: [work]
      direct_notes: false
      pings: true
      max_turns: 10
      cooldown_seconds: 1
      max_backlog: 20
      batch_size: 5
      max_hops: 8
      max_inflight: 1

Board names are exact; an explicit "*" subscribes to currently readable boards, including authorized dynamic-team boards. Own messages and instruction messages do not create observation wakeups. Direct notes and pings are independent switches. Messages written before a subscription's agent exists or before it gains access are not retrospectively queued. Current team history rules still apply when sources are delivered.

Defaults are disabled triggers, 100 turns, zero cooldown seconds, a backlog of 100 references, batches of at most 20 references, eight causal hops, and one inflight turn. Workers serialize turns, so max_inflight currently accepts only one. An explicit smaller backlog also reduces an omitted batch-size default.

The turn budget applies to every dispatch attempt when autonomy is enabled, including explicit instructions, observation wakeups, retries, and skipped/failed attempts. Instructions take priority over queued observations. Resume does not replenish the lifetime turn budget or session deadline. Start a new owner-approved run for a new budget.

That lifetime max_turns limit is distinct from token/cost admission allowances. The owner may explicitly update future token/cost reservations using versioned capacity.update, or shorten admission runtime; it cannot reset consumed turns, refund past reservations or extend the original process deadline. See live resource controls.

docs.title: Durable queue and processing receipts
docs.text:
The broker stores bounded message references in one state record per subscribed agent. Original message content remains in the message store. When a backlog is full, the original message is retained, its wakeup is not queued, and dropped increases. Existing queue entries are retained in order. There is no implicit retry or unbounded overflow queue.

autonomy.status {} is read-only. It returns status.ready, mode, a derived state/reason, pending and inflight counts, turn usage, the next eligible time, drop/suppression counts, a cursor, and bounded processing receipts. Repeated idle discovery changes no durable records or request receipts. suppressed counts queued references removed after they cease to qualify; it is not a complete audit of every unsubscribed message.

pending remains the observation-notification count for compatibility; pending_observations names that count explicitly, while pending_instructions counts queued instruction tasks. When otherwise eligible queued work cannot fit its session or ancestry admission allowance, status reports ready: false, state: "halted", admission_blocked: true, and the existing admission denial in reason and admission_reason. This check reserves no allowance and does not renew any budget.

The cursor advances when a source is scheduled or explicitly acknowledged. Receipts distinguish scheduled, terminal task outcomes, and manual acknowledged processing; they do not establish that a model understood or correctly acted on a message. An agent can acknowledge its currently visible queue through an opaque visible message ID:

{"operation":"autonomy.ack","args":{"message_id":"MESSAGE_ID"}}

worker.next {} is an explicit idempotent mutation. It atomically creates and claims a deduplicated observation task, or claims an existing instruction. It retains the ordinary lease, conversation-readiness, concurrency, runtime, and storage checks. Workers call it only after read-only discovery reports ready.

docs.title: Source privacy and provenance
docs.text:
Observation tasks carry origin.kind: observation and broker-derived source IDs/causal metadata. Their stored task text is a generic notice. Source bodies are resolved separately with read-only wake.read {"id":"TASK_ID"}, using current ACLs, active-agent capabilities, and team history floors. A replayed claim cannot restore revoked source references. If every source is no longer accessible, the worker settles a skipped observation without starting a native model turn.

Automatic source context is bounded to approximately 256 KiB of encoded message data. Remaining queued sources form later tasks. A single oversized source receives an explicit reference-only omission notice and omitted_message_ids; message.get {"id":"MESSAGE_ID"} can retrieve its original content under the normal visibility checks. This keeps automatic framing bounded without silently changing stored messages.

The broker derives causal roots, the parent task, and hop counts from an author's running turn. Callers cannot supply forged provenance in send arguments. A hop limit suppresses further observation wakes; enabled targets also reject instructions beyond their configured hop budget. Root references are bounded to 32 with an explicit truncation flag; task/source edges remain available to reconstruct causality from an owner export. Provenance describes origin rather than privilege.

Source permissions are checked again before delivery and while an observation runs. Revoking access can stop subsequent autonomous execution and deny future reads. It cannot erase context already delivered to a native model or history already written by that model.

docs.title: Owner controls
docs.text:
For a running workspace, inspect the selected agent using its exact state path:

amx managed call autonomy.status --credential-file STATE/owner.json \
  --json '{"agent":"reviewer"}'
amx managed call capacity.get --credential-file STATE/owner.json \
  --json '{"agent":"reviewer"}'

Replace STATE and reviewer with the actual workspace directory and stable agent ID. The terminal workbench and web Session detail view expose the same status; web also reviews effective token/cost admission edits separately from pause.

Read the latest autonomy.status {"agent":"reviewer"} and pass its version to autonomy.control:

{"agent":"reviewer","mode":"paused","version":3}

Only the owner can choose running, paused, or stopped. Pause blocks new dispatch while an existing turn may finish. Stop clears queued wakes and requests cancellation of proposed/running tasks; an active process still requires its stopped acknowledgement. Resume requires fresh capacity, preserves consumed budgets, and does not recreate discarded wakeups. Enabled agents receive their bounded state at initialization/spawn, reserving safety capacity for their first pause/stop before any message arrives. For disabled agents, first use of these optional controls needs normal storage capacity; ordinary credential revocation remains separately reserved. Idle is a derived read-only state.

docs.title: Agentmux Commands
docs.text:
This guide explains what each command is for, when to use it, and the most useful examples.

For a guided native-terminal workflow, see work sessions. For original YAML pane-layout examples, see recipes.

context, observe, task/tasks (including task ID --open), work list --limit and work show --open are included in v0.15.0. These inspection routes have been available since v0.13.0; controllers older than that need an explicit upgrade before they can serve their broker APIs. The v0.14.0 observer adds structured collection diagnostics while preserving schema-1 compatibility.

docs.title: Checked coding requests
docs.text:
demo, work and flow are included in Agentmux v0.15.0. work and flow select a Git project, independently of an interactive workspace's -s NAME selector.

Command Use it to amx demo [--output NEW_DIR] Run a deterministic checked fixture, retain evidence, and apply its patch only to a generated disposable repository; no models amx work "Change description" -- CHECK [ARG...] Preview implementation, fresh review and checks without models or run files amx work "Change description" --allow-models -- CHECK [ARG...] Execute the bounded journey with the explicitly selected provider profiles amx work status [RUN\|latest] Inspect recorded phases, checks, review and next action for the project amx work show [RUN\|latest] Inspect the checked patch preview and retained HTML report path amx work list [--limit N] List retained runs and stable IDs for the selected project; omitted limit retains all history amx work show RUN --open Render a fresh private HTML report from saved evidence and open it in the system browser amx work apply [RUN\|latest] Revalidate and explicitly apply an approved result to the original project amx work recover [RUN\|latest] Resolve an interrupted application's journal against exact source content without replaying its patch

Use --repo DIR for another Git project and --catalog DIR for a custom private history. --output DIR selects a new result directory outside the project; its parent must already exist. Run amx work --help for profile, deadline, attempt, storage, containment and isolation controls. Checks after -- are literal argv; use a check script when shell logic is required. See work on a task for the complete journey and its visual overview.

docs.title: Advanced workflow plans
docs.text:
Command Use it to amx flow run PLAN.json --repo DIR --output RUN Compare independent candidates from one captured revision amx flow mission PLAN.json --repo DIR --output RUN Execute bounded dependency steps and final acceptance checks amx flow watch PLAN.json --repo DIR --output RUN Review stable changed snapshots within duration and run-count limits amx flow lab PLAN.json --repo DIR --output RUN --repetitions 3 Repeat comparisons against a pinned starting snapshot with rotated order amx flow check --repo DIR --checks CHECKS.json --output FILE Record revision-bound executable checks and a private sibling FILE.git fingerprint store amx flow status RUN, amx flow explain RUN Read the saved report, or explain evidence with patch integrity and current freshness amx flow report RUN --output FILE.html Render a private offline report to a new file amx flow handoff RUN [--candidate ID] --output FILE.md Save a private revision-bound handoff brief amx flow apply RUN [--candidate ID] Explicitly apply the selected checked result amx flow recover RUN [--candidate ID] Inspect and resolve an interrupted application

Provider turns require --allow-models; command-only plans and checks can execute owner-selected code without that flag. Plans are strict JSON and choose "execution": "local". Private Git storage is the default and does not confine trusted host execution. Select --isolation bubblewrap for work, or a private plan's isolation object for flow, to require filesystem, PID and network boundaries on Linux. Required boundaries fail closed. Application is separate from execution and never commits or pushes. See advanced workflows for model-free examples, plan fields, exact saved-brief delivery and limitations.

docs.title: Everyday work sessions
docs.text:
Install amx using the release installer or source build. The short command reference covers amx a, ui, ls, link, mode, and directional allow/deny. Everyday commands accept -s NAME for the workspace, before or after the command. Inside an owned tmux attachment the workspace is inferred from that exact attachment; explicit selectors take precedence. Outside, it defaults to work. start / up is the creation exception: its default is always work.

After installation, check command -v amx. With Claude Code and Codex installed and logged in, run amx start from your project directory. It creates the default workspace work and opens its workbench.

Command Use it to amx start Start the default native Claude/Codex team, or attach when that same team is running amx a Restore the last live native terminal, or open the workspace chooser amx split FIRST SECOND Combine existing native terminals in one tmux window amx unsplit ID Return one agent to its own window amx attach AGENT_ID Open one workspace-owned native conversation for direct typing amx dashboard Return to the owner workbench amx web --open Open the local owner app amx add --harness claude --project DIR --title "Task" Start another native session; copy its printed stable ID amx add --harness antigravity --native-only --project DIR Start native Antigravity without an injected Agentmux prompt amx sessions List registered sessions and separately observed external terminals amx context [--json] Explain the ordinary command target, selection source and runtime status without starting anything amx observe [--watch] [--json] [--limit N] Inspect fresh broker/worker reporting, retained task attention and capacity; drill into exact task evidence using the observability guide amx task TASK_ID [--json] Read one delegated instruction, its result, version, delivery and recovery evidence amx task TASK_ID --open Open that exact task in the workbench's Tasks view; recovery still requires explicit review and confirmation amx tasks [--to ID] [--status STATE] [--query TEXT] [--limit N] [--after TASK_ID] [--json] Search retained delegation history, newest first; copy the continuation command to read more amx workspaces [--register DIR] Find named and remembered custom workspaces; register an older custom location amx relaunch AGENT_ID [--resume ID\|last\|picker] [--native-launcher ABSOLUTE_PATH] Relaunch one exited native session, retaining its stable ID and healthy peers; optional launcher recovery applies only to trusted-local interactive sessions amx pair A B [--delivery review\|auto] [--apply] Preview task pairing; --apply atomically configures mutual Commands, both receiver modes and returned results while retaining limits and other permissions amx delivery AGENT_ID [manual\|review\|auto] [--approve CANDIDATE_ID] Inspect native delivery evidence, set receiver mode, or approve an exact queued item; --help lists limits and subscriptions amx connect OBSERVED_ID --title "Task" Prepare a helper for an existing external session; paste the printed setup into its original terminal amx label AGENT_ID "Task" Rename its display title while keeping its ID and conversation amx role AGENT_ID "Role" Change the owner role with CAS; managed workers use it at their next claim, native agents receive an inbox notice amx collaborate AGENT_ID OTHER_ID Give those sessions a dedicated board/memory group and allow notes/pings amx send AGENT_ID "Message" [--mode note\|instruction\|auto] Choose an informational inbox note or an instruction task; auto follows the agent's interaction mode amx inbox Inspect recent coordination and task activity as the owner amx board "Note" --group GROUP_ID Post to a particular collaboration group's board amx reply TASK_OR_MESSAGE_ID "Follow-up" [--mode auto\|note\|instruction] Follow up with broker-validated structured ancestry; shared board posts require --board NAMESPACE or --to AGENT_ID amx isolate AGENT_ID Revoke its peer coordination and memberships across groups; native input stays open amx remove AGENT_ID Close an owned terminal or disconnect an external bridge; retain saved history amx down Stop the workspace's owned processes while keeping saved data

Replace uppercase placeholders with actual paths or IDs. DIR must already exist. --harness chooses the native CLI (claude, codex, pi, or native-only antigravity); --title is a display label and --role supplies optional agent instructions. Choose --native-only to append no Agentmux prompt; it cannot be combined with a nonempty role. Native Antigravity requires this option. Roles never grant coordination permissions. Use role ID "" to clear a coordinated session's role. Session titles can repeat; commands address the stable ID shown under the title. An observed terminal must be connected before its registered ID can be used for collaboration. A prepared bridge does not mean the agent read the pasted setup; external sessions keep their original terminals for typing.

Outside an owned attachment, these interactive commands select workspace work by default, regardless of your current directory. Inside an owned attachment, they infer its checked workspace identity as described above. For another workspace use --session NAME on each command, or select its exact directory with --state DIR. For example:

amx start --session review --project /path/to/project
# In another terminal:
amx attach codex --session review
amx web --session review --open
amx down --session review

send queues coordination. Integrated native sessions can receive attributed turns when their receiver policy is Review/Auto and current permissions allow; Manual remains the default. It never types terminal keystrokes. See native delivery. Use attach to talk directly. With several groups, copy the group ID printed by collaborate or shown under Teams → Owner collaboration groups in the web app. board can choose the only active group automatically; with multiple groups select --group ID or --board NAMESPACE explicitly. Board replies use reply ID "Text" --board NAMESPACE; a private follow-up uses --to AGENT_ID. Direct recipients must already be able to read the referenced message. Broker-inferred thread_id and reply_to retain ancestry without adding a prose prefix. There is no user-supplied thread-root override. For terminal shortcuts, recovery and native history, see work sessions. For bounded headless studies see research.

docs.title: Consented teams and admission controls
docs.text:
Owner collaboration groups created by collaborate are distinct from dynamic consented teams. The latter require teams.enabled and delegated capabilities in the selected managed configuration; the everyday coding preset leaves them disabled. Use amx team --help for the complete command syntax:

Command Behavior amx team list, amx team create NAME Inspect visible teams or create one within configured authority and lifetime limits amx team edit ID --name NAME --description TEXT Change live metadata, retaining the team's ID and namespaces amx team invite ID AGENT, amx team remove ID AGENT, amx team dissolve ID Review membership invitations, revocation or closure as a manager amx team transfer ID AGENT Propose ownership; the proposed owner must accept separately amx team join ID, amx team leave ID, amx team accept-owner ID Decide using --credential-file FILE for the actual acting participant amx team move SOURCE DESTINATION Use the participant's credential and an existing destination invitation to move atomically

Add --session NAME or --state DIR to select the workspace. --version N pins a reviewed version; moves also accept --to-version N. Omitted versions are read once, never retried after a conflict or uncertain response. A human owner cannot impersonate an agent's consent. See dynamic teams.

managed call exposes effective boundaries and capacity through the selected credential. For example, an agent's own shell can run:

"$AGENTMUX_CLI" managed call boundaries.get --json '{}'
"$AGENTMUX_CLI" managed call capacity.get --json '{}'
"$AGENTMUX_CLI" managed call budget.status --json '{}'

These bridge variables are supplied to workspace-native agents. An owner outside their terminal selects --credential-file STATE/owner.json explicitly and can inspect a particular agent with capacity.get --json '{"agent":"AGENT_ID"}'. capacity.update is an owner-only CAS edit of complete admission-budget objects and a shorter admission deadline; it does not rewrite launch configuration, refund past reservations or impose a hard provider bill cap. The terminal B editor and web capacity controls use the same broker rules. See live permissions and resources for fields and constraints.

docs.title: Memory transfers and portable traces
docs.text:
Use managed memory export|import|search|index|prune for explicitly credential- scoped memory operations; memory lifecycle covers CAS, TTL, replacement and asserted import provenance. These are separate from native conversation history.

managed trace list|verify|show inspects owner-accessible local traces. managed trace export --state STATE --agent ID --id TRACE_ID --output NEW_FILE signs a locally verified trace without exporting secret keys. On another machine, managed trace verify-bundle --input FILE --trust OWNER_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256 requires an independently obtained trust fingerprint and no broker state. Use --mac TASK_MAC during local verification/export to pin an existing task anchor. These are owner-exporter attestations, not provider attestations; see traces and recovery.

docs.title: Existing workspace commands
docs.text: The reference below covers the original YAML layout mode (init / load). Its pane IDs, raw terminal input and shared key/value store are separate from the work-session broker's messages, memory and permissions. In particular, dashboard SESSION opens the legacy pane dashboard; use dashboard --session NAME for a managed workbench. Legacy send SESSION PANE -- COMMAND types into a pane, unlike the queued message form above.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
If you only remember a few commands, remember these:

  • templates: show built-in starter configs
  • init: create a new config from a starter
  • load: create a tmux session from a config
  • reload: recreate an existing session from the config
  • status: inspect a live session
  • capture: read output from a named pane
  • send: send text into a named pane
  • edit: reopen the config file

docs.title: templates
docs.text:
What it does: - lists the built-in starter templates that ship with Agentmux - shows friendly aliases like default

When to use it: - when starting a new config - when you forget the built-in template names

Examples:

./bin/amx templates
./bin/amx init coding-starter coding.yaml
./bin/amx init review-starter review.yaml

docs.title: init
docs.text:
What it does: - writes a starter template to a target path - rewrites the top-level session field from the target filename by default

When to use it: - when creating a new config - when you want a starting point instead of hand-writing YAML from scratch

Examples:

./bin/amx init coding-starter coding.yaml
./bin/amx init default my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx init minimal scratch.yaml
./bin/amx init ai-dev work/review.yaml --force

Useful notes: - default is an alias for ai-dev - coding-starter and review-starter are built-in minimal copy-and-tweak starters - --force overwrites an existing file

docs.title: edit
docs.text:
What it does: - opens a config path directly, or - opens the config path remembered for a live session

When to use it: - when editing a config you already have on disk - when you know the session name but do not want to remember where the file lives

Examples:

./bin/amx edit my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx edit my-workflow

Useful notes: - edit <session> works best for sessions created or reloaded through current Agentmux - if metadata is missing, use remember

docs.title: remember
docs.text:
What it does: - attaches a config path to an already-running session without reloading it

When to use it: - when a session is older and missing config-path metadata - when you want edit <session> to work immediately

Examples:

./bin/amx remember my-workflow ./my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx edit my-workflow

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
What it does: - checks YAML shape, references, and config rules - prints errors and warnings without launching tmux

When to use it: - after editing a config - before load if you want a fast safety check

Examples:

./bin/amx validate my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx validate my-workflow.yaml --strict

Useful flags: - --param key=value: override config params - --strict: treat warnings as errors

docs.title: render
docs.text:
What it does: - prints the fully resolved config - prints the launch plan Agentmux would execute

When to use it: - when debugging params, env, cwd, or layout resolution - when you want to inspect what will actually run

Examples:

./bin/amx render my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx render my-workflow.yaml --param project_dir=.

docs.title: pack
docs.text:
What it does: - creates a shareable, self-contained .amx bundle (a ZIP archive) - bundles the configuration file, any local include files, and local scripts

When to use it: - when you want to share a complex agentic team setup with someone else - to distribute workflows that rely on local assets via {{config_dir}}

Examples:

./bin/amx pack my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx pack my-workflow.yaml my-team.amx

Useful note: - .amx bundles can be loaded directly with amx load my-team.amx - you can host .amx bundles online and load them directly from a URL

docs.title: tools
docs.text:
What it does: - generates a JSON Schema export of Agentmux coordination tools - output can be rendered in provider-friendly shapes such as openai, codex, gemini, or claude

When to use it: - when you need a compatibility/debug export of the coordination tool schemas - when comparing Agentmux tool shapes across provider formats

Examples:

./bin/amx tools --format openai
./bin/amx tools --format claude

docs.title: prompt
docs.text:
What it does: - generates the Agentmux operational runtime contract for AI agents - describes either the native MCP tool path or the CLI bridge path, depending on --mode

When to use it: - as the operational system/bootstrap prompt prefix for LLM agents that run inside an Agentmux pane - when you want to inspect the exact coordination contract a pane will receive

Useful note: - this command describes coordination behavior, not necessarily persona delivery - persona may be delivered through a provider channel such as Claude's appended system prompt or a Gemini workspace context file

Examples:

./bin/amx prompt
./bin/amx prompt --provider claude
./bin/amx prompt --provider claude --mode native-mcp
./bin/amx prompt --provider gemini --mode native-mcp

docs.title: tool-call
docs.text:
What it does: - executes a real Agentmux coordination action through a stable JSON envelope - maps canonical tool names like kv_set, wait, or send onto the existing CLI subcommands - accepts payloads from --from-json, --from-file, or --from-stdin

When to use it: - from LLM/provider runtimes that need machine-stable coordination behavior - when you want structured JSON success/error output without scraping human text

Examples:

./bin/amx tool-call kv_set --from-json '{"session":"demo","key":"task","value":"review"}'
./bin/amx tool-call kv_get --from-stdin <<EOF
{"session":"demo","key":"task"}
EOF
./bin/amx tool-call kv_set --from-file /tmp/agentmux-tool.json
./bin/amx tool-call wait --from-json '{"session":"demo","pane":"planner","pattern":"PLAN_READY","timeout":"30s"}'

docs.title: mcp-server
docs.text:
What it does: - exposes the Agentmux tool registry as an MCP stdio server - backs the native MCP integrations for supported providers

When to use it: - indirectly through provider-native launch paths such as Claude, Gemini, or Codex - directly only when testing MCP integration by hand

docs.title: load
docs.text:
What it does: - creates a tmux session from a config or a remote URL

When to use it: - the first time you launch a config - when replacing an existing session from scratch - when launching a shared session from a URL

Examples:

./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx load https://example.com/team.amx
./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml --replace --no-attach
./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml --dry-run

Useful flags: - --replace: replace an existing session - --no-attach: do not attach after launch - --dry-run: print the launch plan only - --verbose: print underlying tmux commands

docs.title: reload
docs.text:
What it does: - reconciles an existing session from a config without destroying the whole session - surgically updates pane metadata or respawns individual panes if their config changed - preserves history and layout for untouched panes

When to use it: - after editing a config for a session that already exists

Examples:

./bin/amx reload my-workflow.yaml --no-attach

Useful note: - unlike load, reload expects the session to already exist - if the session structure (window or pane count) has changed significantly, it falls back to a destructive replace with a warning - if you are running reload from inside one of the session's panes, and that pane's config changed, it will be respawned last

docs.title: list
docs.text:
What it does: - lists tmux session names

When to use it: - when checking whether a session exists - when troubleshooting runtime commands

Examples:

./bin/amx list

docs.title: Runtime Commands
docs.text: These commands operate on live sessions and mostly target named panes.

docs.title: status
docs.text:
What it does: - shows live panes in a session - reports metadata like pane name, title, source, on_exit, current command, and dead - includes PID for running panes and exit status for dead panes

When to use it: - as the first runtime debugging step - to discover pane names - to inspect a single pane with --pane

Examples:

./bin/amx status my-workflow
./bin/amx status my-workflow --json
./bin/amx status my-workflow --pane review
./bin/amx status my-workflow --pane review --json

docs.title: focus
docs.text:
What it does: - switches the active tmux client focus to a named pane

When to use it: - when jumping directly to a pane by name instead of navigating manually

Examples:

./bin/amx focus my-workflow review

docs.title: restart
docs.text:
What it does: - respawns a named pane with its stored startup command

When to use it: - when a pane is stuck or you want to restart its workflow endpoint

Examples:

./bin/amx restart my-workflow review

docs.title: rerun
docs.text:
What it does: - re-executes the stored startup command for a named pane

When to use it: - when you want to re-run the pane’s original command in place

Examples:

./bin/amx rerun my-workflow review

Useful note: - in the current version, restart and rerun are intentionally equivalent

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
What it does: - stops the current pane process - leaves a usable interactive shell in the same pane

When to use it: - when you want to stop a running pane without destroying the layout

Examples:

./bin/amx stop my-workflow review

docs.title: kill
docs.text:
What it does: - destroys the target tmux pane entirely

When to use it: - when you really want the pane removed from the layout

Examples:

./bin/amx kill my-workflow build

Useful note: - this is destructive and can collapse the layout

docs.title: capture
docs.text:
What it does: - reads the current captured output of a named pane

When to use it: - for quick inspection - for small polling scripts - for automation that needs to read pane output

Examples:

./bin/amx capture my-workflow review
./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --tail 20
./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --tail 20 --strip-empty
./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --json --tail 20 --strip-empty

Useful flags: - --tail N: keep only the last N lines - --strip-empty: remove blank and whitespace-only lines - --json: structured output

docs.title: send SESSION PANE -- COMMAND
docs.text:
What it does: - writes text into a named pane - presses Enter by default

When to use it: - when treating a pane like a live workflow endpoint

Examples:

./bin/amx send my-workflow review -- "git status --short"
./bin/amx send my-workflow review --no-enter -- "printf 'queued\n'"

Useful note: - --no-enter stages the text without executing it yet

docs.title: Agentic Commands
docs.text: These commands enable coordination and orchestration between multiple agents.

docs.title: dashboard
docs.text:
What it does: - launches a full-screen, real-time TUI (Terminal User Interface) - provides a "Mission Control" view of all panes, the selected pane's live output, and the shared Blackboard (KV-store)

When to use it: - to monitor an agentic team in real-time - to see live pane activity, including provider MCP/tool traces, without repeatedly running capture and inspect - to see the current state of shared variables without repeatedly running status

Examples:

./bin/amx dashboard my-workflow

Useful shortcuts inside the dashboard: - f: quit the dashboard and attach/switch to the selected pane - r: restart the selected pane - q: quit the dashboard - up/down: change the selected pane and refresh its live output

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
What it does: - provides a deep, comprehensive diagnostic report for a single pane - shows real-time metrics (CPU, Memory), lifecycle metadata (start time, exit code), and recent logs

When to use it: - when a pane is crashing and you need to see its exact configuration and last output - to verify the environment variables injected into a specific agent

Examples:

./bin/amx inspect my-workflow reviewer
./bin/amx inspect my-workflow reviewer --json

docs.title: kv-set
docs.text:
What it does: - sets a shared key-value pair in the session's "Blackboard" - uses tmux session options for storage

When to use it: - to signal state between panes (e.g., status=ready) - to share data like file paths or task IDs

Examples:

./bin/amx kv-set my-team current_task "researching-agent-scaling"

docs.title: kv-get
docs.text:
What it does: - retrieves a value from the session's Blackboard

Examples:

./bin/amx kv-get my-team current_task

docs.title: kv-list
docs.text:
What it does: - lists all keys and values currently stored in the Blackboard

Examples:

./bin/amx kv-list my-team
./bin/amx kv-list my-team --json

docs.title: kv-del
docs.text:
What it does: - removes a key from the Blackboard

Examples:

./bin/amx kv-del my-team current_task

docs.title: wait
docs.text:
What it does: - blocks until a specific regex pattern appears in a pane's emitted output - by default ignores active input/composer text in interactive panes - line anchors like ^...$ work against output lines by default - supports --scope visible for legacy raw screen matching

When to use it: - to synchronize handoffs (e.g., wait for "BUILD SUCCESSFUL") - to wait for real agent output rather than matching text still sitting in the input composer

Examples:

./bin/amx wait my-team builder "SUCCESS" --timeout 5m
./bin/amx wait my-team reviewer '^• REVIEW_DONE$' --timeout 2m
./bin/amx wait my-team builder "SUCCESS" --scope visible --timeout 5m

docs.title: scale
docs.text:
What it does: - dynamically adds or removes instances of a specific agent

When to use it: - to adjust workforce based on load (e.g., spawn 3 more "Researchers")

Examples:

./bin/amx scale my-team researcher 5
./bin/amx scale my-team researcher 1

Useful note: - scaling up creates new panes with unique names like researcher-2 - scaling down removes panes with the highest IDs

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
What it does: - prints environment and dependency information - can check requirements for a specific config file - inspects configured provider CLIs, alias warnings, and likely stale model hints

When to use it: - when tmux or environment issues look suspicious - to verify if a shared config will run on your machine

Examples:

./bin/amx doctor
./bin/amx doctor ./shared-team-config.yaml

docs.title: version
docs.text:
What it does: - prints the current Agentmux version string

Examples:

./bin/amx version
./bin/amx --version

docs.title: --help
docs.text:
What it does: - prints built-in CLI usage

Examples:

./bin/amx --help

docs.title: New workflow
docs.text:
./bin/amx templates
./bin/amx init default my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx validate my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml --replace --no-attach

docs.title: Edit and reapply
docs.text:
./bin/amx edit my-workflow
./bin/amx validate my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx reload my-workflow.yaml --no-attach

docs.title: Inspect and interact with a live pane
docs.text:
./bin/amx status my-workflow --pane review
./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --tail 20 --strip-empty
./bin/amx send my-workflow review "git status --short"

docs.title: Agentmux Config Guide
docs.text:
This guide covers the legacy v1 workspace compiler. Its provider launch flags and raw pane commands differ from v2 managed work sessions. For native interactive teams with authenticated coordination and live boundaries, use work sessions and the managed configuration.

Agentmux configs are local YAML files that define one tmux workspace.

If you want use-case-driven starting points instead of field-by-field reference, see recipes.md.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
• agents: reusable execution defaults
  • windows: layout and context
  • panes: actual runtime units
  • include: reuse parts of other configs

Panes are what really run. Agents help reduce duplication. Windows group panes and provide shared context.

docs.title: Minimal Shape
docs.text:
version: 1
session: my-workflow

layout:
  - window: main
    panes:
      - command: "printf 'ready\n'; exec $SHELL"

docs.title: Common Structure
docs.text:
version: 1
name: My Workspace
session: my-workflow

params:
  project_dir: "."

env:
  PROJECT_DIR: "{{project_dir}}"

agents:
  reviewer:
    provider: codex
    cwd: "{{project_dir}}"
    title: "Reviewer"

layout:
  - window: editor
    root: "{{project_dir}}"
    layout: even-horizontal
    panes:
      - name: editor
        command: "nvim"
        title: "Editor"
        focus: true
      - name: review
        agent: reviewer

docs.title: Reuse and Includes
docs.text:
You can split your configuration across multiple files using the include field. This is useful for sharing common agents, params, or env across different projects.

version: 1
session: project-a

include:
  - shared/base-agents.yaml
  - shared/standard-env.yaml

layout:
  - window: main
    panes:
      - agent: shared-agent

docs.title: Merging Rules
docs.text:
When a file includes another, they are merged with Parent-Wins precedence:

  • params, env, agents: Values in the main file override values in included files.
  • layout: Windows from included files are appended before the windows in the main file.
  • include paths are resolved relative to the file they are defined in.
  • Circular includes are detected and rejected.

docs.title: Requires (Environment Guards)
docs.text:
You can specify mandatory dependencies that must be present before a session is launched. If any env or params are missing, Agentmux will launch an Interactive Setup Wizard to prompt the user for them. If a binary is missing, it will fail fast with a helpful error.

requires:
  binaries:
    - gh
    - nvim
  env:
    - OPENAI_API_KEY
  params:
    - project_name

docs.title: Params
docs.text:
• config params provide defaults
  • CLI --param key=value overrides them
  • Special config_dir: The absolute path to the directory containing the root configuration file is automatically available as {{config_dir}}. Use this to reference local scripts and assets portably.
agents:
  researcher:
    command: "python3 {{config_dir}}/scripts/research.py"

docs.title: Env
docs.text:
Env precedence is:

  • pane env
  • window env
  • agent env
  • session env

docs.title: Working Directory
docs.text:
Working directory precedence is:

  • pane cwd
  • agent cwd
  • window root
  • current working directory where Agentmux was launched

docs.title: Panes
docs.text:
Each pane must specify exactly one of:

  • command: raw shell command
  • agent: reference to a named agent
  • provider: native CLI harness (e.g., claude, antigravity, pi, codex)

Useful pane fields:

  • name: stable runtime identifier
  • title: best-effort pane title
  • persona: path to a Markdown file containing agent instructions
  • model: specific LLM model ID
  • focus: true: start focused here
  • env
  • cwd
  • on_exit

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agents are reusable pane templates, not shared background runtimes.

Current useful agent fields:

  • provider: command (default), shell, ssh, claude, antigravity, pi, gemini, codex, gptme, or aichat
  • aliases: agy -> antigravity, claude-cli -> claude, gemini-cli -> gemini, openai -> codex
  • command: raw shell command
  • persona: path to a Markdown file containing agent instructions
  • model: specific LLM model ID
  • reasoning_effort: optional provider-specific reasoning control for providers that support it
  • cwd
  • env
  • title
  • on_exit

If two panes reference the same agent, you still get two separate pane processes.

docs.title: Native LLM Providers
docs.text:
When you select a native pane provider such as claude, antigravity, pi, or codex, the v1 launcher constructs that CLI's shell command, supplying: 1. Your persona file content through the strongest provider-native surface that CLI actually supports. 2. The amx prompt runtime contract, which carries the operational coordination instructions separately from the persona. 3. Provider-specific launch wiring so persona lands in the strongest available instruction channel for that CLI without pretending every provider has the same system-prompt model. 4. Provider-specific coordination details such as resolved integration mode, tool channel, preferred tool-call input mode, and optional reasoning controls.

Current persona delivery defaults:

  • claude: --append-system-prompt, combining the persona with Agentmux instructions while preserving Claude Code's default system prompt
  • antigravity: interactive bootstrap prompt using the local agy executable
  • pi: --append-system-prompt, preserving Pi's default system prompt
  • gemini: native workspace context file from a session-scoped runtime artifact
  • codex: bootstrap prompt
  • gptme: bootstrap prompt

amx tools --format ... still exists, but it is now an export/debug surface rather than the primary runtime path.

Current integration defaults:

  • claude: prefers native-mcp, falls back to cli-bridge
  • codex: prefers native-mcp, falls back to cli-bridge
  • gemini: prefers native-mcp, falls back to cli-bridge
  • gptme: uses cli-bridge
  • antigravity and pi: use cli-bridge; Agentmux does not change global or workspace MCP settings for these harnesses

Antigravity accepts reasoning_effort: low|medium|high|xhigh|max through --effort. Pi accepts off|minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh|max through --thinking; support depends on the selected model and installed harness version. Pi's model can include a provider prefix, such as anthropic/<model-id>, to select a configured endpoint. Agentmux uses each harness's existing authentication and endpoint configuration and does not copy credentials.

Antigravity and Pi remain ordinary interactive pane processes in this launch mode. Their CLI bridge runs coordination commands through the harness's shell tool, subject to its permissions. A launcher is not a structured input channel or an isolation boundary. See harness integration for capabilities and limits.

Codex-specific runtime notes:

  • Agentmux launches Codex with --no-alt-screen to behave better inside tmux panes and preserve scrollback.
  • The v1 launcher uses --sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval never. This is specific to the original pane mode. Everyday v2 local interactive work sessions preserve native approval/sandbox configuration; see work sessions.

Direct pane provider: usage is intended for native providers. Command-style providers like ssh should be defined on an agent alongside command:.

Example: 

agents:
  expert:
    provider: claude
    persona: "prompts/expert.md"
    model: "sonnet"
    reasoning_effort: "high"

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
Supported layouts:

  • even-horizontal
  • even-vertical
  • main-horizontal
  • main-vertical
  • tiled
  • grid

Exact grids use:

layout:
  - window: workspace
    layout: grid
    grid_rows: 2
    grid_columns: 2
    panes:
      - command: "nvim"
      - command: "go test ./..."
      - command: "git status"
      - command: "printf 'review\n'; exec $SHELL"

docs.title: Exit Behavior
docs.text:
Supported on_exit values:

  • shell
  • remain
  • restart
  • kill

Typical use:

  • shell: default interactive behavior
  • remain: keep finished output visible
  • restart: auto-restart a watcher-like pane
  • kill: remove the pane when the command exits

docs.title: Good Workflow
docs.text:
Create from a starter:

./bin/amx init default my-workflow.yaml

Then iterate:

./bin/amx validate my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx render my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml --replace --no-attach
./bin/amx reload my-workflow.yaml --no-attach

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
See:

  • testdata/examples/minimal.yaml
  • testdata/examples/ai-dev.yaml
  • testdata/examples/on-exit.yaml
  • testdata/examples/review-loop.yaml
  • testdata/examples/ssh-ops.yaml

docs.title: Bounded spawning and dynamic teams
docs.text:
Agentmux can let an authorized agent request a child worker, create a team, and invite collaborators. These features are off unless explicitly configured. Roles and self-declared leadership never grant runtime authority.

Agent-created teams use invitations and participant consent. They are separate from owner-created collaboration groups configured with collaborate/Connections; see live permissions. Both expose scoped boards/memory, but joining a team never grants instruction authority. Everyday interactive sessions can keep their native terminals throughout; work sessions cover launching and attaching them.

Start with the bounded team configuration:

From the repository root, build with make build first. This fixture uses a custom state path, so keep --state /tmp/amx-teams on subsequent owner commands:

./bin/amx managed up examples/managed/bounded-teams.yaml --state /tmp/amx-teams --broker-sandbox bubblewrap

The example has lead, peer, the static team board, shared memory findings, and an approved helper template. Its /bin/cat fixtures make no model calls; they echo tasks and do not independently decide to recruit collaborators. The broker, static agents, and spawned helpers use Bubblewrap; working Linux namespace support is required.

docs.title: Owner policy and child capabilities
docs.text:
The relevant configuration is:

spawn:
  enabled: true
  allow:
    lead: [helper]
  templates:
    helper:
      harness: command
      command: [/bin/cat]
      sandbox: bubblewrap
      network: none

teams:
  enabled: true
  creators: [lead]
  history: since-join   # default; "all" is an explicit alternative

limits:
  max_runtime_seconds: 600
  max_concurrent_tasks: 4
  max_spawns: 4
  max_spawn_depth: 1
  max_teams: 4
  max_team_members: 4

Templates are immutable owner-approved process definitions. A spawn request selects a template and concrete capabilities; it cannot supply executable text, a new endpoint, mounts, credentials, or an arbitrary workspace. Spawn templates must use bubblewrap and receive a fresh workspace and identity. Model access and networking come from the template; network: host means unrestricted network access, while none keeps the network namespace separate.

Using the lead's credential:

./bin/amx managed call agent.spawn \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/lead.json \
  --request-id recruit-helper-1 \
  --json '{
    "template":"helper",
    "capabilities":{
      "boards_read":["team"],
      "boards_write":["team"],
      "memory_read":["findings"],
      "targets":[{"to":"peer","actions":["message.send"]}],
      "join_teams":true
    }
  }'

The response contains the new agent ID and redacted registry metadata, not its credential. With managed up, the supervisor adds a worker window and the worker runs each accepted task in its own sandbox. With manual managed serve, registration alone does not create a tmux worker; the owner must start its worker or use the supervised launch path.

Supported capability fields are:

Capability Delegates boards_read, boards_write Exact existing board namespaces. memory_read, memory_write Exact existing shared-memory namespaces. targets Concrete peer IDs and message.send, ping.send, or instruct actions. spawn_templates Named templates the parent is already allowed to recruit. create_teams Explicit authority to create new team namespaces. join_teams Explicit authority for a child to accept eligible invitations; false by default.

Requested rights must fit the parent's delegable authority and session policy. A child does not inherit static wildcard ACLs. Its namespace and target access remain subject to the parent's effective rights. A parent may control its own child; a child may send a note or ping back but cannot instruct its parent merely because it was spawned. Recruiting a child does not renew the persisted run deadline, create unlimited resources, or grant provider-spending guarantees.

Creating a new team is a deliberate resource-creation exception: an agent with create_teams may create a fresh board/memory namespace and become its owner. That does not confer access to an existing unrelated namespace or change any agent-to-agent instruction edge.

docs.title: Invitations, consent, and versions
docs.text:
Create a team with the lead credential:

./bin/amx managed call team.create \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/lead.json \
  --json '{"name":"Review group"}'

The result supplies the team id, current version, dedicated board, and shared-memory namespace memory. An agent creator becomes the first member. The human owner can administer teams without impersonating a participant.

Copy the returned team ID, then invite the peer using the current version:

./bin/amx managed call team.invite \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/lead.json \
  --json '{"id":"TEAM_ID","agent":"peer","version":1}'

# After that invitation, use the version returned by it (normally 2).
./bin/amx managed call team.join \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/peer.json \
  --json '{"id":"TEAM_ID","version":2}'

An invitation requires the manager to be allowed to message the invitee. The invitee accepts using its own credential; an invitation does not silently enroll it. Static participants can accept permitted invitations when teams are enabled. A spawned child additionally needs delegated join_teams, and its parent must currently have the relevant membership/access. A child cannot accept an unrelated invitation to bypass its parent's namespace limits. Parent departure removes the dependent child's effective access too. The explicit team-creation right above governs an authorized child's own newly created team.

team.list returns teams visible to the caller: those it owns, belongs to, or is invited to. The human owner can inspect all teams. Use it to obtain current versions before mutations:

./bin/amx managed call team.list \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/lead.json --json '{}'

Membership mutations use compare-and-set versions. Concurrent changes produce conflict; read the current team before issuing a new decision. Reuse the same request ID and arguments when recovering an uncertain response to an existing write, rather than issuing a second logical invitation or removal.

Operation Arguments Authority/effect team.create name, optional description Owner or configured/delegated creator; creates a new team. team.invite id, agent, version Team manager; creates a pending invitation. team.join id, version The eligible invitee; records its consent. team.remove id, agent, version Team manager; removes a member or pending invitee. team.leave id, version A member/invitee leaves or declines. team.dissolve id, version Team manager; closes the team and future namespace access. team.update id, version, name, description Manager changes live metadata without changing namespace identities. team.transfer id, version, agent Manager proposes a current authorized member as owner; no authority changes yet. team.accept-owner id, version Only the proposed owner consents; current authority and delegation are rechecked. team.move id, version, to_id, to_version A non-owner member consumes its destination invitation and leaves the source atomically.

The manager is the human owner or the current team owner. An owner transfers ownership (with the new owner's separate consent) before leaving, or dissolves the team. A proposed owner appears in pending_owner; a removed invitee/member loses that proposal. Delegated children cannot use transfer to invent missing team-creation authority. Transferring to the human owner uses the literal ID $owner and the owner credential must accept. Team membership enables its scoped board and memory; it does not grant instruct, interrupt, spawn, or access to another team's data. Voluntarily following a proposal on a board is agent behavior, not an administrative privilege grant.

docs.title: Everyday control and live inspection
docs.text:
amx team list --state /tmp/amx-teams
amx team create "API investigation" --description "Temporary joint review" --state /tmp/amx-teams
# Replace TEAM_ID below with the ID returned by create:
amx team edit TEAM_ID --name "API review" --description "Owner-approved scope" --state /tmp/amx-teams
amx team invite TEAM_ID lead --state /tmp/amx-teams
amx team invite TEAM_ID peer --state /tmp/amx-teams
# Each invited agent runs this with its own credential, if it consents:
"$AGENTMUX_CLI" team join TEAM_ID --credential-file "$AGENTMUX_CREDENTIAL_FILE"
# After lead has joined, the owner proposes a transfer:
amx team transfer TEAM_ID lead --state /tmp/amx-teams
# Lead, as the proposed new owner, separately accepts:
"$AGENTMUX_CLI" team accept-owner TEAM_ID --credential-file "$AGENTMUX_CREDENTIAL_FILE"
# A non-owner member may move only after a separate destination invitation:
"$AGENTMUX_CLI" team move SOURCE_ID DESTINATION_ID --credential-file "$AGENTMUX_CREDENTIAL_FILE"

team join, leave, accept-owner and move require an explicit acting credential. The simple CLI fetches omitted versions once, submits one decision, and never retries a conflict or uncertain write. Add --version N and, for move, --to-version N to pin previously reviewed versions. Team moves require a pending destination invitation, the participant's own consent, valid parent access and both current versions; any failure rolls back both memberships and the invitation. Owners cannot force another participant's consent.

The terminal Teams view uses e to edit metadata and t to propose its selected member as owner. Reviews freeze IDs and versions, and native terminals remain interactive throughout. The proposed agent accepts through its own tools. Owner inspection includes each member's effective access; each participant sees only its own self_access reason and blocking ancestor. Recorded membership alone never asserts effective authority.

The web Groups & teams view edits names/purposes, reviews invitations and ownership proposals, and accepts an ownership proposal addressed to the human $owner. It never accepts on an agent's behalf. Drafts retain their original version; concurrent edits require explicit version review or discard before saving.

capacity.get {} and identity.capacity report remaining lifetime spawn/team counts, spawn depth, available template names, current team slots (including reserved invitations), admission deadline and inherited admission denials. These are read-only snapshots, not reservations: concurrent decisions may consume a slot before the next mutation. Revoking an agent or dissolving a team does not refund lifetime counts. Live permissions and resource controls describes owner CAS admission-budget edits and effective-versus-stored access.

Inspect the fixture's lead capacity without reserving anything:

amx managed call capacity.get --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/owner.json \
  --json '{"agent":"lead"}'

The web Session detail view exposes these values and separately reviews changes to effective session/agent admission budgets and a shorter admission deadline. The owner response for capacity.get {} includes the effective session budget; an inspected agent response includes its effective agent budget. All edits use resource_version; stale reviews cannot adopt another client's new version.

docs.title: History, memory, and departure
docs.text:
teams.history: since-join is the default. New members can read team-board messages posted after their most recent join, rather than the whole historical conversation. Rejoining begins a new history window. history: all explicitly permits members to read earlier team-board messages.

Author receipts are an exception: agents can still retrieve messages they authored through their visible-message feed. Existing direct-recipient receipts also retain their own visibility rules. Leaving or removal revokes future team reads/writes; it cannot erase content already delivered or retract a participant's own sent-message record. The human owner remains trusted with the complete durable state. A query restricted to a board still requires current board access.

Shared memory is the team's current knowledge state, not a historical message stream. A newly admitted member can read current shared-memory entries, including entries created before it joined. Message-history filtering is not a guarantee that current memory, quoted messages, or artifacts contain no older information. Treat memory promotion and sharing as part of the scenario's information policy.

docs.title: Stopping and inspecting agents
docs.text:
The owner can inspect the registry with agent.list. A parent/ancestor can stop its descendants; the owner can stop any configured agent:

./bin/amx managed call agent.stop \
  --credential-file /tmp/amx-teams/credentials/lead.json \
  --json '{"id":"CHILD_ID"}'

Stopping revokes that agent's and its descendants' credentials and fences their work. It reports process_stopped: false: authorization revocation is not proof of OS-process termination. The supervisor interrupts the affected workers, and a running worker fails closed when its next authenticated task observation is rejected. For an uncertain turn, confirm the process is stopped before resolving or retrying its task. Agent IDs and pane positions are separate identities.

The runtime bounds concurrent tasks, lifetime spawning, spawn depth, teams, membership, records, requests, and elapsed run time. Usage reported by a provider is observational; these limits do not imply a hard token/dollar cap. All of these features remain optional, and their security depends on the chosen sandbox: local participants retain trusted host access.

For repeated controlled comparisons, use the research runner and its dynamic population admission rules. The separate single-task experiment runner disables dynamic spawning and teams; its simpler schema does not model those treatments.

docs.title: Evaluate Agentmux against alternatives
docs.text: Agentmux has no established public task-quality ranking. A passing regression suite establishes the exercised implementation behavior. It does not show that an Agentmux team produces better patches, saves time or costs less than one coding agent or another orchestrator. scripts/benchmark-managed.py measures logical broker API throughput; it does not measure native agent task quality or simultaneous model-worker scale.

docs.title: First verify the evaluator without models
docs.text:
The matched-attempt runner requires Linux, Git and Python with pidfd support. Process tracking bounds active identities and each observation scan separately. Kernel-confirmed exited identities release tracking slots; an unreadable process record does not prove exit. Cleanup and supervision failures remain attempt failures, even if a patch passes its task contract. Run from a checkout:

python3 scripts/test-compare-workflows.py
python3 scripts/test-summarize-comparison.py
python3 examples/evaluation/run-offline-controls.py --output /tmp/amx-controls-NEW

Choose a new output path. The control suite creates a tiny pinned source repository and runs deterministic actors that produce a correct artifact, produce an incorrect artifact while exiting zero, exit nonzero with a correct artifact, and exceed their deadline. It verifies that failures remain failures, unknown usage/cost remain unknown, and the original Git state and dirty files are preserved. controls-result.json is a harness test result, not an AI benchmark. Its deterministic actors are not Agentmux or competitor results.

docs.title: Declare a matched live comparison
docs.text:
Copy the example plan outside the checkout and replace every placeholder. It deliberately refuses to run until a real local repository and full commit object ID are supplied. The tiny normalization task and example grader illustrate the interface; they cannot support general coding-quality claims.

Use a preregistered task set that includes representative bug fixes, tests, refactors and changes spanning files. Include a single-agent baseline, Agentmux and named alternatives relevant to the intended workflow. Record exact tool/wrapper versions and hashes, model names/settings, authentication route, machine, dependencies, task selection and exclusion rules before execution. Freeze checks before viewing results. Every task needs evaluator-selected independent checks; a model's completion message is never the result authority. Keep disclosed development checks separate from held-out grading. Each independent check declares absolute evaluator_files outside the source repository. The runner pins their resolved paths and content hashes before any arm starts and rejects changed evaluators before or after grading. Include the grader and every grading dependency you own. Merely running a project test inside the actor-writable repository is a development check, not an independent oracle. This detects changed pinned files; it does not sandbox graders or hide their contents from a trusted local arm. Grading must inspect without changing the candidate files. The runner hashes all candidate files and symlink targets, excluding the root .git metadata, before and after each check and invalidates a check that changes them, including a grader that repairs an incorrect answer before exiting zero. Traversal does not follow symlinks and has the same file-count/byte/deadline bounds. Put test caches and generated outputs outside the candidate repository; Python bytecode writing is disabled for invoked commands. The fingerprint is content evidence, not isolation against an independent hostile host writer.

Each arm is an executable argv list. {repo} names a newly initialized private Git repository containing the same pinned source files, {task} names a JSON file with the task ID, prompt and optional disclosed development_check, and {output} names its private artifact directory. Substitutions never invoke a shell. Wrappers must work in the supplied repository, save relevant evidence, return their actual status and finish with the proposed patch in that repository. They must not push or merge into the original project. The example Agentmux adapter runs amx work and explicitly applies its checked result to that disposable repository; applying to the study copy is part of that arm's timed workflow. You supply pinned single-agent and competitor wrappers for the chosen native CLIs/SDKs.
