default gives you the fuller ai-dev template with a session name derived from coding.yaml.

Fastest copyable file:

  • docs/recipes/coding-starter.yaml

Typical next steps:

./bin/amx validate coding.yaml
./bin/amx render coding.yaml
./bin/amx load coding.yaml --replace --no-attach

What to customize first:

  • params.project_dir: set the repo path you want to work in
  • agents.coder.command: point to the local coding model or shell command you actually use
  • agents.reviewer.command: point to your preferred review command
  • pane name fields: add stable names if you want runtime control

Typical shape:

version: 1
session: coding

params:
  project_dir: "."

agents:
  coder:
    provider: command
    command: "ollama run codellama"
    cwd: "{{project_dir}}"

layout:
  - window: workspace
    root: "{{project_dir}}"
    layout: grid
    grid_rows: 2
    grid_columns: 2
    panes:
      - name: editor
        command: "nvim"
        focus: true
      - name: tests
        command: "go test ./... -count=1"
      - name: git
        command: "git status"
      - name: coder
        agent: coder

Good runtime loop:

./bin/amx status coding
./bin/amx capture coding tests --tail 20 --strip-empty
./bin/amx send coding coder "Summarize the current diff"

Related files:

  • testdata/examples/ai-dev.yaml

docs.title: Review Session
docs.text:
Use this when you want a dedicated code-review workspace with an editor pane, a reviewer pane, and a checks pane.

Best starter:

./bin/amx init review-starter review.yaml

Fuller starter:

./bin/amx init review-loop review.yaml

Fastest copyable file:

  • docs/recipes/review-starter.yaml

Typical next steps:

./bin/amx validate review.yaml
./bin/amx load review.yaml --replace --no-attach
./bin/amx status review

What to customize first:

  • agents.reviewer.provider: choose an installed native CLI such as codex
  • agents.reviewer.model: optionally select a model supported by that native CLI/account
  • the checks pane command: swap npm test for the command your repo actually uses

Typical shape:

version: 1
session: review

params:
  project_dir: "."

agents:
  reviewer:
    provider: codex
    cwd: "{{project_dir}}"

layout:
  - window: review
    root: "{{project_dir}}"
    layout: even-vertical
    panes:
      - name: diff
        command: "git diff --stat"
      - name: reviewer
        agent: reviewer
      - name: checks
        command: "npm test"

Good runtime loop:

./bin/amx focus review reviewer
./bin/amx send review reviewer "Review the current diff for regressions"
./bin/amx capture review reviewer --tail 40 --strip-empty
./bin/amx rerun review checks

Related files:

  • testdata/examples/review-loop.yaml

docs.title: Remote Ops Session
docs.text:
Use this when you want one tmux session for a remote shell plus supporting local panes.

Best starter:

./bin/amx init ssh-ops ops.yaml

Typical next steps:

./bin/amx validate ops.yaml
./bin/amx load ops.yaml --replace --no-attach
./bin/amx status ops

What to customize first:

  • agents.prod-shell.command: replace the placeholder SSH target
  • any supporting panes: logs, health checks, deploy scripts, or dashboards
  • pane names: give the important panes stable names so you can target them later

Typical shape:

version: 1
session: ops

agents:
  prod-shell:
    provider: ssh
    command: "ssh user@prod.example.com"
    title: "Prod"

layout:
  - window: ops
    layout: even-horizontal
    panes:
      - name: prod
        agent: prod-shell
        focus: true
      - name: logs
        command: "tail -f /var/log/syslog"
      - name: checks
        command: "printf 'run health checks here\\n'; exec $SHELL"

Good runtime loop:

./bin/amx status ops
./bin/amx capture ops logs --tail 40 --strip-empty
./bin/amx focus ops prod

Related files:

  • testdata/examples/ssh-ops.yaml

docs.title: Watcher Session
docs.text:
Use this when you want panes that behave differently when their startup command exits.

Best starter:

./bin/amx init on-exit watcher.yaml

What this starter demonstrates:

  • shell: run once, then drop into a shell
  • remain: keep finished output visible
  • restart: automatically rerun the command
  • kill: remove the pane after the command exits

Useful commands while testing it:

./bin/amx load watcher.yaml --replace --no-attach
./bin/amx status watcher
./bin/amx capture watcher watcher --tail 20 --strip-empty
./bin/amx restart watcher watcher

Related files:

  • testdata/examples/on-exit.yaml

docs.title: Coordinated Team
docs.text:
Use this when you want multiple agents to work together using shared state and synchronization.

Best starter:

./bin/amx init supervisor-demo team.yaml

What this starter demonstrates:

  • Shared Blackboard (KV-Store): Agents reading and writing to amx kv-set.
  • Synchronization (Wait): One agent waiting for another to print a specific message.
  • Dynamic Scaling: A manager agent expanding the team automatically.

Typical next steps:

./bin/amx load team.yaml
# Observe the manager pane coordinating the engineer panes

Key coordination commands:

# Set a shared variable
./bin/amx kv-set my-team current_task "research"

# Wait for a pane to finish
./bin/amx wait my-team worker "DONE"

# Scale the workforce
./bin/amx scale my-team worker 5

Related files:

  • testdata/examples/research-team.yaml

docs.title: Choosing A Starter
docs.text:
For authenticated native conversations and opt-in collaboration, begin with amx start and the optional verification walkthrough. If you specifically want a v1 custom layout:

  • use default for day-to-day coding
  • use review-loop for dedicated code review
  • use ssh-ops for remote shell workflows
  • use on-exit when testing watcher and restart behavior
  • use minimal when you want the smallest possible starting point

List all starters:

./bin/amx templates

docs.title: Releasing Agentmux
docs.text: Release from a reviewed main revision after its CI, installed first-run and documentation checks pass. A versioned release must include the commands and behavior promoted by its README and installation guide.

docs.title: Prepare and validate
docs.text:
1. Choose a new version; never move an existing published tag. Update the changelog, versioned installation commands and release description together.
  2. Run relevant regressions and the comparison harness's offline controls. Confirm the Linux and macOS Installed first run jobs pass. Those jobs package all four supported archives, verify their checksums, install the host binary and complete amx demo through actual workflow evidence.
  3. Review the source archive and distribution contents for private data. Include contribution/security instructions, the MIT LICENSE file and docs/third-party-notices.txt.
  4. Merge the reviewed revision and create the new version tag on that exact commit. Pushing a v* tag starts the release workflow.

Release and installed-artifact jobs use Go 1.27.3; the regular test job retains Go 1.24 to check the minimum source-compatibility promise. Use a maintained Go release when updating the distribution toolchain. Regenerate and check dependency notices for that exact toolchain before building.

From a source checkout, use the selected release toolchain:

python3 scripts/check-third-party-notices.py --go /path/to/go1.27.3 --write
python3 scripts/check-third-party-notices.py --go /path/to/go1.27.3 --check

The explicit source selection covers runtime modules for all four targets, Go's runtime/vendor notices and included Unicode data. A missing component, changed upstream notice or changed dependency version requires review and regeneration. The check never rewrites the notice automatically.

The default release targets are Linux and macOS on x86-64 and ARM64. Native execution in CI covers the runner architectures only; verifying a cross-built archive's contents is not execution on that architecture. Full Bubblewrap isolation is tested separately on Linux.

docs.title: Publication gates
docs.text:
The release workflow first checks tag freshness and existing publication state. A complete published release is a successful no-op; an unfinished release requires inspection and is never overwritten automatically.

GoReleaser creates an unpublished draft containing the four archives and checksum manifest. scripts/smoke-release.py installs the host archive through the normal checksum/version verifier and runs help, workflow discovery and the deterministic demo. It requires passing revision-bound checks and a confirmed application receipt, and retains private evidence in smoke.json.

scripts/publish-release.py then checks that every uploaded asset digest matches the local verified bytes and rechecks the remote tag before publishing the draft. Failed or uncertain verification leaves the draft unpublished. Inspect the workflow and release state before resolving or retrying an interrupted run.

docs.title: Verify delivery
docs.text:
Download the published host archive and checksums.txt using the installer or authenticated GitHub tooling as appropriate for repository access. A complete independent smoke run needs all four platform archives:

gh release download v0.15.0 --repo pagel-s/agentmux --dir /tmp/amx-v0.15.0-artifacts
python3 scripts/smoke-release.py --artifact-dir /tmp/amx-v0.15.0-artifacts \
  --version v0.15.0 --output /tmp/amx-v0.15.0-installed-check

The final v0.12.0 archives predate the MIT license file and remain verifiable. New builds and snapshots must include LICENSE and docs/third-party-notices.txt in every platform archive.

Choose new directories for every run. The smoke command never replaces an existing installation and never makes model calls. Its passing result covers the installed deterministic journey; native providers need their own recorded checks. A checksum is consistency evidence against the release manifest, not an independent signature.

If a published release is defective, create a new version. Preserve the prior tag and assets, and document the affected behavior and upgrade path.

docs.title: SSH workers and broker scale
docs.text:
managed remote runs one configured worker on an explicitly selected trusted Linux amd64 SSH host. It deploys the Agentmux binary, a reduced definition with only that agent's process/connection and accessible board names, and that agent's own credential. It never copies owner credentials, SQLite, peer credentials, source workspaces, dependency directories or native login caches. The remote host can read that worker's token/data and must be trusted for them.

Start the local broker, submit a task, then run:

amx managed remote --state STATE --agent worker --host YOUR_SSH_ALIAS \
  --remote-dir /tmp/my-agentmux-worker --once

The directory must be new and absolute with an existing canonical parent; it is created privately and retained for inspection/history. The worker requires Bubblewrap and its native harness/dependencies on the remote machine. Python 3 and SSH Unix-socket forwarding are required. No root privileges or public broker port are used. The owner's local process keeps the SSH session open; disconnect/owner cancellation stops the remote worker's process group. Broker lease checks stop native execution when communication cannot be confirmed.

An SSH remote Unix-socket forward exposes only the authenticated local broker socket inside the remote private state. Each sandbox still receives only its own token. network: none therefore permits broker coordination without providing ordinary IP connectivity. Provider traffic needs an explicit host or allowlist network policy separately.

Use --layout layout.json for explicit host-specific paths:

{
  "workdir": "/tmp/my-agentmux-worker/state/workspaces/worker",
  "read_only_paths": ["/opt/my-native-harness"],
  "auth_file": "/private/remote-native-credential.json"
}

The optional command array changes argv only for a command harness. Layouts cannot change the role, model, policy or broker admission limits. Dependencies and native credentials must be provisioned separately; selecting auth_file does not copy a local login. Default workspaces are dedicated remote paths. Disk capsules require their exact state-owned workspace layout. The broker remains authoritative after deployment: managed claims capture the current owner role, and live permission/admission overlays apply centrally. Changing a remote layout is not a way to override those controls. Filtered native file credentials are reloaded between managed turns from the selected remote source; this does not synchronize a local owner's later login refresh.

To restart an identical deployment, add --resume. It validates private owned directories and exact binary/definition/credential hashes before execution, preserving workspace and native session files. Changes to credentials, binary, definition or layout require an explicit new deployment/migration; they are never overwritten implicitly. The central session deadline is not extended. Use owner task/conversation recovery before resuming uncertain work.

Remote tracing is rejected when trace.enabled is selected: the local broker cannot authenticate a remote trace through a local file path. A central trace collector is a future extension; this command does not claim that coverage. Portable signed trace bundles support moving already captured local evidence for offline verification; they do not add remote capture or collection. See traces and recovery. Spawning remains centrally bounded, with the existing local supervisor creating approved child workers. This is explicit SSH placement, not an automatic multi-host cluster scheduler or host failure migration service.

docs.title: Reproducible validation
docs.text:
python3 scripts/smoke-managed-remote.py --host YOUR_SSH_ALIAS \
  --remote-dir /tmp/amx-unique-check --output /tmp/remote-result.json
python3 scripts/benchmark-managed.py --output /tmp/broker-benchmark.json
python3 scripts/soak-managed.py --output /tmp/soak-result.json

The remote smoke test exercises command-only board/memory handoff, credential separation, forbidden reverse instructions and resumption of an identical remote deployment. It makes no provider calls. Use a disposable remote directory and retain its report to inspect the boundaries on your selected host.

The benchmark measures authenticated board/memory operations against a durable SQLite broker. Report host/storage conditions, workload, logical client count, latency and errors alongside any throughput measurement. Logical API clients do not represent simultaneous native model processes or maximum cluster capacity. Small teams remain the primary deployment target.

The bounded soak checks completed task anchors, broker restarts and an in-flight crash. Uncertain native work requires explicit resolution without automatic replay. Passing a finite check does not establish multi-day uptime, remote host failure migration or availability for other deployments.

docs.title: Research environment mechanics
docs.text: The owner-controlled environment validates choices and computes outcomes. Models choose actions; they do not supply verdicts or payoffs. The existing public-goods-v1 game is described in research.md. This guide covers the second game and opt-in coalition/population mechanics.

docs.title: Repeated trust and resource exchange
docs.text:
Run the command-only protocol example:

amx research plan examples/research/trust-exchange.yaml
amx research run examples/research/trust-exchange.yaml --output /tmp/amx-exchange
amx research analyze /tmp/amx-exchange --behavior-csv /tmp/amx-exchange-behavior.csv

trust-exchange-v1 has two economic stages per round:

  1. Invest. Each actor privately learns its own current productivity (an integer from two through game.multiplier, at most four). It may communicate and form consented teams if permitted, then submits {"to":"other-actor","amount":2} or {"to":null,"amount":0}. The nonnegative integer amount must fit its current wallet and per-round cap. It is immediately deducted from that wallet. The recipient receives sender-specific escrow equal to investment times the recipient's hidden productivity. All investments commit at one barrier.
  2. Return. Each actor privately sees incoming escrows and chooses {"returns":{"sender-id":3}} or {"returns":{}}. Each repayment must fit that particular sender's escrow. The recipient keeps the rest; there is no enforced repayment promise. Actual repayments and retained value enter the respective wallets and affect next-round capacity. Invalid returns burn all incoming escrow, rather than silently granting a successful transfer.

Invalid investments/returns each cost one available wallet credit, or one utility point if the wallet is empty. The same credit is not charged twice. Individual utility is the round's net wallet change minus any such empty-wallet penalties. Shared/individual/winner point rules are applied to the resolved utilities. New private productivity is sampled each round. The owner retains the entire hidden schedule outside participant workspaces.

Outputs include every actual investment, multiplier, escrow, repayment, retained amount, burned amount, validity decision, wallet balance, utility, and payoff. Return fraction is measured against total created escrow. Public-goods funding metrics are not meaningful for this exchange game; use welfare and transfer/ repayment metrics. Scripted baselines are all-defect, seeded random choices, and an informed cooperative strategy that invests with a productive partner and returns escrow. These are explicit comparators, not a proof of optimal strategy.

preregistration.primary_outcome: escrow_return_fraction selects the run's returned/received-escrow fraction for paired and factorial estimates. A run with no received escrow has no return-fraction observation; it is excluded rather than treated as zero. Analysis reports the resulting metric-specific sample sizes and warns that treatment can change this denominator. Public-goods funding outcomes are rejected for this environment. See the complete outcome definitions and design controls.

The example's deterministic participants exercise real broker invitation, voluntary acceptance, private channels, and objective transfers. Their chosen 50% repayment policy tests mechanics; it is not language-model behavior.

docs.title: Explicit consented reward pools
docs.text:
Set teams: true, visibility: direct, and team_rewards: pool to allow score pooling. During an action/return stage an actor may include "reward_team":"team-id". The ID must identify an active team in which that actor was a member at the frozen end-of-coordination/investment snapshot.

Pooling occurs only when at least two eligible members independently select the same team. Each actor selects at most one pool, so overlapping memberships cannot double-count utility. The selected members' utilities are summed and divided equally into scoring utilities, then the declared point rule is applied. Raw wallets and social welfare do not change. Outputs record raw and scoring utilities plus the actual pool members and totals. A lone selection has no effect. An unauthorized/stale nonmember selection is invalid. With team_rewards: none, membership creates channels without redistributing points.

The snapshot defines economic eligibility for that stage; subsequent membership changes do not retroactively change the settled rule. Actual board/memory access still follows current broker membership and its revocation rules.

docs.title: Declared dynamic populations
docs.text:
amx research run examples/research/dynamic-population.yaml --output /tmp/amx-population

The default is a fixed population with spawning disabled. Opt in explicitly:

population:
  mode: dynamic
  max_agents: 3
  entry_credits: 1

The managed source team must contain approved spawn templates and parent/template allowlists. Research preserves those controls, including parent capability subsets, sandbox boundaries, depth, and lifetime spawn limits. Templates have autonomous wakeups disabled. A registered child receives no research turn until the next round boundary. At that boundary the environment admits it only when its parent can transfer entry_credits from its own remaining wallet. No additional capital is minted. The transfer allocates existing endowment and reduces the parent's future spending capacity; it is not retroactively scored as a prior-round investment. A child lacking funding remains deferred.

Population snapshots record actor IDs, parents, entry transfers, deferrals, and retirement. Retired wallets remain frozen rather than being reminted. Private observations and hidden cases are extended for admitted actors, and all workers at the next phase use that declared snapshot. Current-version limits impose a conservative lifetime ceiling as well as the active cap; stopping a child does not replenish spawn slots. The minimum active game population is two, maximum 16. The plan reports a worst-case task count using the maximum population.

Participants must let the owner issue all phase tasks. An extra parent-issued child instruction is detected as an out-of-protocol pending task and interrupts the attempt. Revocation/transport uncertainty during an active phase also fails closed; it is not silently converted into a missing decision or replay. Broker spawning can register a child during a turn, but activation and new observations remain at the next-round barrier.

Dynamic composition is an explicit treatment, not a hidden change to a fixed study. Spawn identities and timing are not seeded. Replaying an exact dynamic trajectory requires its recorded population/coordination history in addition to the environment seed. Baselines currently use the initial fixed population; they do not model endogenous birth/retirement strategies. Comparing different population paths therefore requires a separately declared analysis and resource normalization.

The same owner console exposes current population, phase tasks, teams and capacity. Phase pause/step/stop and explicit steering remain available; interventions are recorded and assisted runs are excluded from default estimates. Team metadata edits, ownership proposals and participant moves use the ordinary consent and version rules. They do not override research phase barriers or turn a child into a funded participant before its declared admission boundary.

docs.title: Plan and run a controlled study
docs.text: Use a declared design to compare coordination conditions while keeping the participant population, environment and execution settings explicit. Research supports behavioral primary outcomes, role/personality prompt profiles, one-to-six-factor designs and Latin-square scheduling. The command-only role/personality example lets you inspect those controls without provider calls.

docs.title: Define the question and controls
docs.text:
The factorial pilot example crosses individual/shared points with consented private-team permission off/on. Public board/direct messaging, roles, native tool permissions, resource limits, game mechanics and conversation mode stay fixed. Permission is the treatment; participants decide whether to create, invite or join a team. A helper does not choose their strategy or force a coalition.

Declare the question, primary outcome, hypotheses, complete factorial cells, ordered factor levels, fixed controls and analysis before collection. Choose sample size using the intended inference and report complete paired blocks. The example is a small feasibility design; it is not a powered behavioral study. The runner rejects missing/duplicate cells, undeclared factor changes and varying extra instructions. Prompt treatments do not establish intrinsic agent traits.

Keep model assignments and tool permissions explicit. A fixed mixed-model dyad supports comparisons within that population; it does not rank the models. A private channel for two agents may overlap with already permitted direct communication, narrowing the intervention being tested. For broader conclusions, consider larger populations, multiple environments, counterbalanced actor/model assignments and independent scoring.

docs.title: Prepare and inspect without model calls
docs.text:
python3 scripts/research/prepare-study.py --output /tmp/amx-study-input
amx research plan /tmp/amx-study-input/study.yaml

Preparation discovers installed code dependencies and selects explicit private native credential files. It does not generate responses, log in, install packages or mount a whole host home. Configure executable/auth/model paths with its flags and inspect the generated study before starting. Native monetary options and usage reports do not establish actual charges or a total bill cap; one task may contain several provider calls. The durable ledger limits task starts across completion, failures and interrupted reruns.

docs.title: Collect and inspect observations
docs.text:
Use the same frozen executable and inputs for the collection so rebuilds cannot change broker/worker code between cells. Select available models explicitly and verify their tools and isolation separately before consuming the study budget. Then opt into native turns:

amx research run /tmp/amx-study-input/study.yaml \
  --output /tmp/amx-native-study --allow-models
amx research analyze /tmp/amx-native-study --csv /tmp/amx-native-summary.csv \
  --behavior-csv /tmp/amx-native-behavior.csv

The runner has no output-dependent early stopping or automatic native retry. Failures and invalid game actions are reported separately. Infrastructure uncertainty, budget exhaustion and deadlines interrupt collection and preserve artifacts. Do not rerun an uncertain native turn as though it never happened.

Private artifacts include the preregistration/hash, immutable world truth, exact task payloads, behavior IDs, objective actions/costs/payoffs, reported native usage, preflight versions/executable hashes, broker coordination and analysis. Keep these records with the study. Raw owner/agent state and native authentication caches can contain sensitive data; review exports before sharing.

Report paired main effects and interactions with their assumptions, intervals, complete block counts, invalidity, execution failures and actual team formation. Check extraction against adapter-visible final answers before interpreting behavioral outcomes. An operationally complete run can still have inadequate measurement validity or statistical power.

docs.title: Trace and continuation safeguards
docs.text:
New native research turns require trace.enabled: true for every participating native agent and eligible spawn template. Preparation sets this explicitly. Traces retain adapter-visible event boundaries for final-answer extraction; malformed non-JSON framing is a protocol failure. Trace capacity is finite and exhaustion stops execution. Trace coverage does not reveal hidden reasoning or provider-internal context.

Execution provenance records the decision protocol and hashes of the runner, worker/broker executable, native entrypoints and regular absolute file arguments. Continuation checks that fingerprint before starting more turns, including at phase boundaries. Credentials can refresh independently; the fingerprint does not pin provider weights, all imported dependencies, remote infrastructure or the kernel.

Completed phase evidence must match its declared configuration, trial and durable task reservations. Duplicate or inconsistent result cells are rejected. Analysis reports descriptive quality warnings and complete paired-block counts. Missing traces, invalid actions, failures and inadequate sample sizes still limit interpretation when collection completes.

docs.title: Finite multi-agent research environments
docs.text: amx research runs repeated-round environments with private observations, scarce resources, validated decisions, and live objective payoff feedback. It complements the single-task experiment pilot. Built-in environments are public-goods-v1 and trust-exchange-v1; the exported Scenario / Episode interfaces separate owner-controlled mechanics from participant observations. See exchange, reward pooling, and population mechanics and planning a controlled study.

docs.title: Run the no-model protocol smoke
docs.text:
Build Agentmux, inspect the entire execution matrix, then run the included deterministic command participants:

make build
./bin/amx research plan examples/research/public-goods.yaml
./bin/amx research run examples/research/public-goods.yaml --output /tmp/amx-research
./bin/amx research analyze /tmp/amx-research
./bin/amx research analyze /tmp/amx-research --csv /tmp/amx-research-analysis.csv

Run these commands from the repository root. Later examples use amx on your PATH; see installation. plan validates and prints the trial matrix and task counts without starting participants. run occupies its terminal until completion; use another terminal to observe it.

Use a new short private output path; directories are 0700, artifact files 0600, and Unix socket paths must fit within 100 bytes. The CSV must be a new file. Linux Bubblewrap with working unprivileged namespaces, Python 3, and the current Agentmux binary are required. This example makes zero model calls.

The example schedules six independent runs, each with three participants and two rounds. Every round has a coordination task and a decision task per participant: 72 command tasks in total. All workers and each broker are independently sandboxed. Alice creates a real broker team and invites Bob; Bob accepts using his own credential, then writes a receipt to the team's private board. Charlie does not become a member. These are deliberately scripted strategies that test the protocol, not evidence of intelligent self-organization.

docs.title: Observe and intervene live
docs.text:
Research uses the same terminal and web owner consoles as other managed work. The runner prints the exact current state path and console commands when a new attempt becomes ready. The private output's live.json points to that attempt. To open the controls before the first participant phase:

amx research run examples/research/dynamic-population.yaml \
  --output /tmp/amx-live-study --start-paused

# In another terminal; OUTPUT follows the current attempt:
amx research status /tmp/amx-live-study
amx research watch /tmp/amx-live-study --follow
# Use the exact STATE printed by the runner:
amx dashboard --state STATE --view research
amx web --state STATE

OUTPUT means the study's top-level output directory (here /tmp/amx-live-study); STATE means one attempt's broker directory printed by the runner. status and watch accept either. OUTPUT resolves the most recently published attempt. Add --follow to watch the complete study across trial transitions. Dashboard/web start with an exact STATE; use study follow in Events or the web Research view to observe the matrix. Web follow switches snapshots with attempt-fenced controls, while terminal opening of another attempt is explicit. Before the first attempt is ready, there may be no live pointer yet. A missing live.json alone does not establish a failed run; check the runner terminal.

status prints one JSON snapshot. watch prints JSON snapshots as they change and exits when the attempt finishes or is no longer live. Ctrl-C in the watcher stops observation while the runner continues. Closing a dashboard or stopping the web process also leaves the runner running. watch OUTPUT --follow stays open through gaps until all trials complete or you interrupt it. Stopped, interrupted and incomplete attempts are labeled explicitly; missing results do not establish that a runner is executing. Use research study OUTPUT for overall status and research history OUTPUT for paginated archived evidence.

Final-phase controls also apply at the transition between trials. An accepted stop finishes the current phase and prevents the next trial. Pause and an already-consumed step initialize the next attempt paused. Without --start-paused, an unused step admits exactly one phase there; --start-paused takes precedence and pauses every new attempt. Carried controls appear as audited interventions before worker admission. If the entire study has no remaining phases, it can complete without waiting for another step. Completion atomically acknowledges the latest control version, so a racing accepted stop cannot be lost.

Study status and archived history validate the saved plan against the frozen manifest. Omitted, reordered or relabeled trials are rejected instead of changing completion counts or silently skipping evidence.

The terminal Events view and web Research view show trial/condition, round and phase, population, authoritative phase-task delivery, finite deadline, reserved model-task count and requested versus acknowledged control versions. A fresh runner heartbeat is separate from a responsive broker. A stale/unknown heartbeat does not establish that a task stopped. Heartbeats are ephemeral, consume no durable request receipts, and become unknown after broker restart.

Pause, resume, single-phase step and stop require the displayed control version and an explicit reason. In CLI JSON, use result.research.control.version from a fresh status response; do not use the progress revision or acknowledged version. For example, after reading version 2:

amx research step /tmp/amx-live-study --version 2 \
  --reason "Inspect team formation after one phase"

Fetch status again before the next control, because accepted changes advance the version. A conflict means review the current state before submitting again. Use research resume OUTPUT --version N --reason "..." to release a paused live runner; this does not restart a stopped or interrupted runner.

These controls act at phase barriers. A phase already admitted may finish; cancellation of accepted tasks is a separate action in Tasks. A step admits exactly one phase and then waits. Pausing never renews the trial deadline or model budget. --start-paused pauses each new attempt and is itself an intervention. Transport failures never trigger automatic write replay or model reruns.

Teams exposes real agent-created teams, invitations awaiting participant consent, membership versions and scoped board/memory. Owner invite/remove/dissolve actions are reviewed against exact IDs and versions; the owner never impersonates an agent's acceptance. Spawned children appear with template and parent; admission to a dynamic study still happens only at the next-round boundary. Permission versions change with membership so revoked shared knowledge is not presented as currently readable. Previously delivered context cannot be erased.

Observation alone does not mark a run assisted. Every explicit phase control, and successful owner changes to messages, knowledge, permissions, teams or tasks, are recorded separately from authenticated runner scheduling and participant activity. Results retain the intervention journal and owner-mutation count, and default condition/paired/factorial/per-agent estimates exclude these exploratory runs. intervened_runs reports them, and behavior exports carry an intervened flag. New evidence is checked against both its private intervention artifact and the durable broker checkpoint; missing metadata does not silently become clean evidence. This provenance assumes a trusted host owner.

After broker shutdown, the web/terminal console can show saved research metadata without enabling writes or claiming live execution. The local read authenticates the original owner token; credential rotation and damaged state still fail closed. research status OUTPUT and research status STATE both distinguish live and saved metadata. When the broker is unavailable, they authenticate and read the saved broker checkpoint; cached live.json content is not the status authority. Saved status reports live: false and no current runner heartbeat, and does not restart workers or prove their processes stopped.

Research participants use bounded headless managed turns. There is no native terminal to type into during those turns; such a configuration is rejected before execution. Use the normal interactive workspace for native conversation. Within a study, steer through explicit phase controls, scoped notes/knowledge or task cancellation. Extra owner instruction tasks interrupt the finite phase protocol rather than quietly becoming unscheduled model work. Broker and adapter-reported traces do not expose hidden model reasoning or unreported tools.

docs.title: The environment and actual incentives
docs.text:
Each round has two projects. Every participant privately receives one bit. XOR of all participants' bits identifies the productive project. An individual clue alone is incomplete. New bits are generated for each round from an owner-held seed; the seed, other clues, and future cases are not put in participant prompts or environment variables. Hidden ground truth stays outside broker state and participant workspaces. Seeds reproduce environment cases, not native model sampling or communication timing.

Each agent starts with a finite credit balance. Its decision must be exactly:

{"project": 0, "contribute": 2}

or a valid zero contribution:

{"project": null, "contribute": 0}

Project is 0 or 1; contributions are integers within both the per-round cap and the agent's remaining balance. Unknown or duplicate keys, extra text/fences, missing fields, and overspending are invalid. The environment charges every valid contribution permanently, including money spent on a wrong or unfunded project. Only the productive project pays a dividend, and only if contributions reach its threshold. Every valid participant receives that dividend, including a valid zero contributor. This creates a concrete free-rider opportunity.

Individual utility is dividend received minus contribution. Invalid or failed decision tasks receive no dividend, utility -1, and lose one remaining credit when available. An exhausted balance cannot go negative; the utility penalty still applies. Invalid execution is recorded separately from intentional zero contribution. The declared reward rule computes and accumulates actual points:

Reward mode Points credited each round shared Total participant utility divided equally among participants. individual That participant's own utility. winner One point split among those tied for highest strictly positive utility; otherwise zero.

Agents are told to maximize their final cumulative points under that rule. They receive the resolved productive project, all actions and validity, actual costs, remaining balances, utilities, round points, and cumulative points before the next round. The reward mechanism therefore affects subsequent decisions; it is not a label added after the run. Points are experimental scores, not external monetary payments. Team membership adds private collaboration channels and does not silently pool rewards or confer command authority. Explicit team_rewards: pool allows mutually selected members to pool scoring utilities; wallets and raw objective welfare remain separate and are recorded.

docs.title: Scheduling and information boundaries
docs.text:
The runner creates every participant's private observation, commits all phase instructions, then starts one managed task turn per participant concurrently. It waits for every worker to stop before passing the phase barrier. It then repeats this for sealed action tasks and resolves all contributions together. Participants cannot read other participants' task results before resolution. They can voluntarily communicate through allowed broker channels. Native conversation mode is fresh by default. An explicitly configured conversation: persistent retains that participant's private native history between phases within the same trial; the mode is captured in the resolved configuration and should be held constant across a comparison. Launch order is seeded and recorded; exact process start time and asynchronous message order are not controlled. Coordination outputs are supplied back to that participant for its decision, alongside public previous-round feedback.

Conditions choose visibility: isolated, board, or direct. Isolated removes shared boards/memory and direct communication. Board gives a common research board/memory namespace. Direct additionally preserves only the source team's explicit message.send / ping.send edges. No participant receives instruction rights over another. Original source workdirs and namespace ACLs are replaced; agent roles and declared runtime dependencies are captured as potential confounds. Autonomy wake subscriptions and spawning are disabled so extra turns cannot cross the phase barriers. Population is fixed by default. Explicit population.mode: dynamic admits approved broker-spawned children only at the next-round boundary, within declared resource and actor caps; see the mechanics guide for entry-credit transfers and protocol-deviation handling.

With teams: true in a direct condition, all participants may create teams and use existing invitation/consent/CAS rules. Actual memberships, invitations, and private boards remain broker-authorized. Full team snapshots are captured at phase barriers; each decision receives only its own memberships. Team changes and private communication are observable coordination events, not invented coalition labels. See dynamic team semantics, including since-join message history. Members can still communicate/change membership during a decision turn; that ordering is retained in the coordination trace.

Every run gets fresh broker credentials, workspaces, private homes, and local/ shared memory, including between conditions. Native model participants must use Bubblewrap. Custom command participants may explicitly use trusted local mode; that mode cannot establish hostile-agent information confidentiality. The default broker mode is Bubblewrap; broker_sandbox: local explicitly trusts the host broker. Read-only dependencies cannot contain the current owner output or an ancestor. Keep declared dependencies code-only; external services, shared files, native auth accounts, and configured environment values can still create confounds and belong in the study design.

docs.title: Manifest, baselines, and analysis
docs.text:
Manifests require version: 1, a conservative id, a managed team path, bounded trials / seeds, randomization_seed, trial and phase timeouts, game options, and explicit conditions. Unknown nested fields and multiple YAML documents fail. Planning makes no participant/provider calls. Every condition appears once in each seed/repetition block, in a deterministic randomized order by default. Runs execute serially; participants within a phase execute concurrently. The sample varies both visibility and reward to cover implementation paths. It is not a causal comparison: use a declared factorial or vary one factor at a time for a study.

Three independent scripted comparators run against exactly the same hidden cases and resource accounting: all-defect, seeded random actions, and an informed cooperative oracle that funds the productive project when feasible and immediately socially beneficial. The oracle comparator is a declared strategy, not a proof of optimal long-horizon planning. Its choices are never supplied to participants. The generic Scenario / Episode contracts allow additional versioned environments without delegating ground-truth scoring to a model.

Optional counterbalancing: latin_square assigns cyclic condition orders over the seeded, shuffled seed/repetition blocks. Every condition occupies every serial position equally; trials * len(seeds) must be divisible by the condition count, so a partial cycle is rejected. The base condition permutation is seeded, and the exact schedule is frozen in plan.json. This balances serial positions; it does not promise first-order carryover balance or seed native model sampling. Omitting the field retains the historical randomized plan and manifest hashes.

Named role_assignments replace the source role for the specified initial actor IDs in that condition. Unspecified actors retain their source roles. Named personality_profiles append a declared behavioral prompt to the specified actors. Select profiles with condition fields role_assignment and personality; unknown profiles/actors and empty prompts fail validation. The controlled-game protocol remains appended to every role. These are prompt treatments, not personality measurements. Profile labels and exact text are frozen in the manifest; the resolved prompt/configuration is hashed separately for every trial. Spawned participants retain their declared template role; initial-actor assignments do not implicitly alter descendants.

See the role/personality pilot for a complete two-factor manifest with reversed role assignments and exact order counterbalancing. Its scripted participants ignore prompt treatments, so it tests collection mechanics only. A model study must separately choose adequate independent blocks, provisioning and a native-turn budget before execution.

Try that design without any model calls, from the repository root:

amx research plan examples/research/roles-personality.yaml
amx research run examples/research/roles-personality.yaml \
  --output /tmp/amx-role-profile-pilot
amx research analyze /tmp/amx-role-profile-pilot \
  --csv /tmp/amx-role-profile-summary.csv \
  --behavior-csv /tmp/amx-role-profile-behavior.csv

This schedules 16 command-only trials and 192 task turns, with four complete paired blocks. The selected outcome is observed consented-team count; analysis labels the scripted, tiny pilot and its unmet 20-block preregistered minimum. Use new output/CSV paths when changing the design. To study real participants, prepare a separate managed team and manifest, inspect its plan, provision the exact harness/model/auth/isolation choices, declare a positive native-task budget, and explicitly opt in with --allow-models.

Analysis reports objective welfare, funding rate, credits spent, invalid decisions, valid zero contributors on funded rounds, failed tasks, and actual teams with multiple members, plus baseline welfare. Pairwise contrasts align condition runs by seed and repetition. Preregistered designs support one to six binary factors and require every factorial cell exactly once per block (at most 64 conditions). Factors are reward_mode, visibility, teams, team_rewards, role_assignment and personality. Undeclared changes to any of these factors or extra condition instructions are rejected. Main effects and every declared interaction use complete paired blocks, averaged over other factor levels. Per-decision behavior IDs, model/harness labels, and separate validity/execution-failure fields support reproducible behavioral coding. Per-agent uncertainty uses run-level means rather than treating rounds as independent samples.

preregistration.primary_outcome selects the metric for condition primary_outcome_estimate, paired_primary_outcome_difference_to_minus_from and all factorial paired_effect estimates. Each effect names its outcome. Legacy welfare summary/contrast fields retain their original meaning. An unregistered exploratory manifest can select top-level primary_outcome; conflicting top-level and preregistered choices are rejected. The default remains total_social_welfare. Supported run-level outcomes are:

Primary outcome Definition total_social_welfare Sum of objective round welfare. productive_project_funding_rate Fraction of rounds funding the productive project; public-goods only. total_credits_spent Sum of objective round credit costs. invalid_action_count Sum of invalid decisions across rounds. funded_zero_contributors Sum of valid zero contributors on funded rounds; public-goods only. teams_with_multiple_members Distinct active teams with at least two members observed at phase barriers; repeated snapshots count once. Teams created and dissolved between snapshots are not counted. failed_task_count Phase tasks not submitted or verified. Infrastructure uncertainty still interrupts collection. escrow_return_fraction Total escrow returned / total escrow received over the run; trust-exchange only. Runs with zero escrow are unavailable, not zero, and are excluded from this metric and its paired contrasts.

The escrow denominator can be affected by treatment; analysis explicitly warns about this selection and reports metric-specific sample sizes. It must be read alongside investment/escrow activity. Research CSV keeps its original leading columns and appends primary outcome, mean and sample size; analysis_json retains all contrasts, uncertainty, preregistration and evidence warnings.

Every unregistered collection is labeled exploratory. Analysis flags any scripted command participants, incomplete evidence coverage, owner intervention, and fewer than eight complete paired blocks. Eight is an explicit descriptive disclosure threshold, not a power calculation or a claim that eight is enough. Preregistered minimum-block shortfalls also retain their dedicated warning; meeting that minimum does not establish adequate statistical power.

Sample standard errors and unadjusted 95% Student-t intervals are descriptive and assume independent runs; repeated worlds, provider dependence, order, and uncontrolled model sampling can violate that assumption. No automatic trait classification, causal conclusion, significance claim, or power calculation is made. Define behavioral outcomes and hypotheses before collecting model data. The critical values follow NIST's Student-t table, rounded upward, with degrees of freedom capped at 30 for conservative larger- sample bounds. Tiny-sample or degenerate intervals do not establish stability.

docs.title: Models, artifacts, failures, and resuming
docs.text:
Replace the command fixture team with native managed harnesses and verified dependency/auth provisioning. The mixed harness acceptance documents real Claude/Codex/Pi boundaries and native-tool policy. Run planning first: repeated rounds use two turns per agent, so model studies can be costly. Actual native execution additionally requires explicit --allow-models, a strict preregistration, and positive budget.max_model_tasks:

amx research run /private/study.yaml --output /tmp/amx-model-study --allow-models

Agent count, roles, harness/model versions, native permissions, tools, context, and provider settings should be held constant across an incentive comparison. Otherwise those differences compete with the proposed explanation. The runner uses explicit phase observations and feedback with fresh native turns by default or the configured within-trial persistent conversation; it does not claim to capture every native model context, tool read, or hidden state. There are no automatic runner task retries and no billing guarantee from reported usage. A durable ledger reserves every native task before workers start, including interrupted attempts. Resuming or rerunning cannot reset that budget; an absent/corrupt ledger fails closed. Task counts bound native turns, not the number of provider requests a native harness may make within a turn.

The private output contains the normalized manifest/configuration and hashes, balanced plan, executable hashes and nongenerative version/auth/isolation preflight, owner-only ground truth, baseline trajectories, exact phase instructions and results with reported usage, objective round transitions, owner-call JSONL, complete paginated broker record export, final results, and descriptive analysis. These files contain private messages/observations, model outputs, and configuration. Review/redact them before sharing. CLI run/analyze output is the descriptive aggregate, not the private observations. behaviors.jsonl contains deterministic per-decision IDs and objective fields. Export those rows separately without raw prompts:

amx research analyze /tmp/amx-research --behavior-csv /tmp/amx-behavior.csv

The overall trial and each phase have finite deadlines, including phase task queuing, with a bounded cleanup window after workers stop. Native failures are recorded and invalid actions are scored under the declared rule. Worker or transport uncertainty interrupts the attempt; it never becomes an invented decision or an automatic model rerun. The runner joins workers and stops the broker on exit. To continue a study after the runner has exited, invoke the same research run MANIFEST --output OUTPUT command again, retaining --allow-models for native studies. It skips completed trials and runs those not yet started. This differs from research resume, which only releases a live pause. A partial or uncertain attempt requires stopping any remaining processes and explicitly choosing a fresh attempt with --rerun-interrupted:

amx research run examples/research/public-goods.yaml \
  --output /tmp/amx-research --rerun-interrupted

Reruns create new attempts and preserve old evidence. A changed manifest or resolved team cannot reuse an existing output. This prevents quiet reuse of cross-condition memory and accidental replacement of failed observations. Persistent native histories fail closed after a failed/interrupted begun turn; if later phases would need that blocked history, the run interrupts for explicit owner resolution rather than silently resetting or starting a fresh history.

Behavior CSV schema 2 also retains selected projects/partners, received escrow, reward pools, parent IDs and phase-task references without prompts. Population policy is verified against the frozen manifest; dynamic trajectories carry an initial-fixed-population baseline scope and comparability warnings. See the control center guide.

docs.title: Legacy pane runtime guide
docs.text:
These commands address original v1 layouts on the default tmux server. For current authenticated workspaces use work sessions: dashboard --session NAME, attach ID --session NAME, relaunch ID, and down --session NAME. Native session IDs, layout pane names and provider-native conversation IDs are different identifiers.

Agentmux runtime commands operate on live tmux sessions through stable named panes.

docs.title: Runtime Model
docs.text:
• sessions are tmux sessions
  • panes are the runtime control unit
  • pane name is the stable identifier
  • tmux metadata stores runtime details like source type, startup command, and config path

If you want live control, give panes explicit name: fields.

docs.title: Core Runtime Commands
docs.text:
Status:

./bin/amx status my-workflow
./bin/amx status my-workflow --json
./bin/amx status my-workflow --pane review

Focus:

./bin/amx focus my-workflow review

Restart and rerun:

./bin/amx restart my-workflow review
./bin/amx rerun my-workflow review

Stop and kill:

./bin/amx stop my-workflow review
./bin/amx kill my-workflow build

Capture output:

./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --tail 20 --strip-empty

Send input:

./bin/amx send my-workflow review "git status --short"
./bin/amx send my-workflow review --no-enter "printf 'queued\n'"

docs.title: Status Data
docs.text:
status exposes live pane metadata including:

  • window and pane indexes
  • pane ID
  • pane name
  • pane title
  • source_type
  • agent_name
  • configured on_exit
  • current foreground command
  • dead state

That makes it possible to inspect finished remain panes, restart loops, and normal interactive panes through Agentmux instead of raw tmux commands.

docs.title: JSON Mode
docs.text:
Runtime JSON output uses stable envelope fields:

  • schema_version
  • kind

Important commands:

  • status --json
  • capture --json
  • action commands like focus --json or send --json

Runtime JSON errors are also structured and keep the same exit codes as plain-text mode.

docs.title: Config Path Metadata
docs.text:
When you load or reload a config from disk, Agentmux remembers the config path on the live tmux session.

That enables:

./bin/amx edit my-workflow

If a session is older and missing that metadata, backfill it:

./bin/amx remember my-workflow ./my-workflow.yaml
./bin/amx edit my-workflow

docs.title: Blackboard (Shared KV-Store)
docs.text:
The "Blackboard" is a shared memory layer for agent coordination. It uses tmux session options to store key-value pairs that are accessible from any pane in the session.

Set a value:

./bin/amx kv-set my-workflow current_task "fixing-auth-bug"

Get a value:

./bin/amx kv-get my-workflow current_task

List all values:

./bin/amx kv-list my-workflow
./bin/amx kv-list my-workflow --json

Delete a value:

./bin/amx kv-del my-workflow current_task

This lets tmux pane processes signal progress and share values without a broker. It provides neither per-agent authorization nor filesystem isolation.

docs.title: Synchronization (Wait)
docs.text:
The wait command blocks until a specific pattern (regex) appears in a pane's output. This is useful for coordinating handoffs between agents.

./bin/amx wait my-workflow reviewer "REVIEW COMPLETE" --timeout 5m

If the pattern is found, the command exits with code 0. If the timeout is reached, it exits with code 1.

docs.title: Dynamic Scaling (Scale)
docs.text:
The scale command allows you to dynamically adjust the number of instances of a specific agent in a running session.

# Increase or decrease the number of 'researcher' workers to 3
./bin/amx scale my-workflow researcher 3

This command will: - Scale Up: Create new panes using the agent's original configuration (command, env, cwd) from the session's config file. - Scale Down: Terminate instances of the agent until the target count is reached. - Naming: Automatically assign unique names like researcher-2, researcher-3. - Layout: Re-apply the window's defined layout (e.g., even-horizontal) to keep the workspace tidy.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Missing session:

./bin/amx list
./bin/amx load my-workflow.yaml --replace --no-attach

Missing pane:

./bin/amx status my-workflow

Missing config-path metadata:

./bin/amx remember my-workflow ./my-workflow.yaml

Useful debugging commands:

./bin/amx doctor
./bin/amx status my-workflow --json
./bin/amx capture my-workflow review --json --tail 20 --strip-empty

docs.title: Trust boundaries and validation scope
docs.text: Managed mode remains experimental. Agentmux has separate execution boundaries for managed teams, native terminals and owner-driven coding workflows. Managed policy is enforced by the broker; Linux Bubblewrap supplies the selected worker and broker boundaries. Native terminals retain their provider's approvals. The work and flow commands select workflow isolation separately and do not inherit managed sandbox settings. Local execution retains trusted host authority.

docs.title: What must be trusted
docs.text:
The owner, host administrator, kernel, Agentmux executable and chosen sandbox tools are trusted. The owner selects executable code, native authentication, mounts, endpoints and policy. Someone able to change owner state, executable code or the host kernel is outside the isolation threat model. Bubblewrap is not a separate virtual machine or a defense against a compromised kernel.

Native providers and remote SSH host administrators are separate trusted parties for the data and credentials deliberately supplied to them. Private local history does not establish provider-side deletion or confidentiality. Native login snapshots may be readable by the worker they authenticate; avoid sharing a credential that gives more provider authority than that worker needs.

docs.title: What the runtime enforces
docs.text:
Boundary Enforcement Evidence and limits Agent identity and coordination Individual credentials, broker-side authorization, separate note/ping/instruction rights, board and memory scopes Adversarial broker tests exercise denied reads/writes, revoked membership, cached requests and private history. An agent can still try to persuade a permitted recipient through message content. Live owner policy Versioned overrides, independent collaboration contributions, isolation overlays and explicit review of ambiguous legacy grants Group overlap, deny/reset, migration rollback and stale-version tests preserve unrelated intent. Roles and titles grant no authority. Local processes can still bypass API ACLs through host access. Dynamic organization Owner-approved spawn templates, child permission subsets, finite spawn resources, consented membership and history floors Spawn/team integration checks use real sandboxed workers. Team membership does not implicitly grant instruction authority. Execution attempts Instance-bound leases checked before launch, during monitoring and before completion Regressions replace a task lease before launch and while a real subprocess runs. Stale workers stop and cannot complete the replacement attempt. Monitoring cannot undo side effects already in progress. Native results Required native completion records, strict protocol handling and complete stdin delivery Recorded/fake native streams exercise missing, malformed and conflicting results. Installed provider smoke checks are listed separately in provider compatibility; protocol fixtures do not certify every future CLI release. Filesystem and resources Explicit mounts, separate histories, optional capped tmpfs capsules and cgroup limits Actual namespace, ENOSPC, cgroup exhaustion and descendant cleanup checks are available. Requested unsupported boundaries fail closed. Cgroup checks require a delegated user manager and are distinct from namespace checks. Managed network destinations Independent network namespace and an explicit destination proxy in allowlist mode Integration checks reject direct routes and proxy opt-out. CONNECT/SNI checks leave encrypted HTTP authority and paths opaque. network: host grants host networking explicitly. Restart and uncertain delivery Durable state, preserved deadlines, charged retry attempts and explicit owner resolution The model-free soak injects a broker crash and rechecks completed task anchors after recovery. Operators must stop old processes and inspect side effects before requesting a retry. Admission and portable evidence Permanent declared turn reservations, versioned live overlays, local HMAC traces and owner-signed portable bundles Admission is not a provider bill cap. Bundle verification requires an independently obtained owner-key fingerprint and authenticates that owner's attestation, not provider identity or output truth. Research records Native traces, execution fingerprints, fixed plans and durable native-turn reservations New native turns require trace coverage. Continuation checks reject changed execution provenance; legacy completed results remain readable. Local evidence is not an external immutable attestation.

Revoking an agent fences work addressed to that agent and its descendants. Instructions already accepted from that issuer to other active agents remain durable tasks. Use task.cancel explicitly to withdraw those instructions; issuer revocation is not a retroactive cancellation of everything it requested. Broker permissions govern API operations. They do not guarantee how an LLM interprets instructions embedded in otherwise permitted messages; a recipient's tools and sandbox still need appropriate limits.

Replies derive ancestry from a visible broker message and check the outgoing audience; a reply never grants access to an ancestor. Imported memory retains the authenticated destination author plus explicit archive-source claims. Those claims and archive checksums are not authenticated source identities. See memory lifecycle, live permissions and portable traces.

Native interactive input and managed task execution have separate boundaries. The opt-in native delivery bridge rechecks recipient policy, sender authority and source visibility before reserving an attributed turn. Transport acceptance, execution evidence and task verification remain separate. Supported cancellation only targets the correlated peer turn; Claude's already queued inbox turns cannot be retracted. Manual native input retains the provider's own approval and execution behavior. An interactive native_only session omits Agentmux prompt injection; a live role edit sends a broker notice rather than keystrokes. Relaunch requires an exited workspace-owned native session and an explicit history choice when resumption is desired. It preserves identity and deadlines without asserting that provider-side history or billing is controlled by the broker.

docs.title: Coding workflow boundaries
docs.text:
amx work and amx flow run owner-selected commands and native tools in separate Git worktrees. Worktrees separate changes; private snapshot storage separates Git objects from the source repository. Neither alone restricts host filesystem or network authority. Required PID containment stops namespace descendants but also needs full isolation to restrict files and networking.

Full Linux workflow isolation requires working user, PID, mount and network namespaces and capped private HOME/tmp filesystems. Native tools receive their assigned workspace and selected runtime dependencies; review workspaces are read-only. Checks receive no provider credentials or network. Workspace growth has no hard disk quota. Requested boundaries fail closed.

Workflow allowlists use a different, inspecting proxy from managed egress. A per-turn ephemeral CA lets it check every HTTPS HTTP/1.1 Host or HTTP/2 authority, while upstream certificate/hostname checks remain enabled. Only the public CA enters the sandbox; its signing key remains in controller memory. Opaque tunnels and HTTP upgrades are refused. Certificate-pinned, mutual-TLS or incompatible custom-trust clients can fail closed. Grants still select origins, not individual URL paths. See full workflow isolation and managed destination controls.

The workflow controller and any selected host inference bridge remain trusted. Selected credentials are explicitly filtered for a candidate; managed broker ACLs are not workflow tool permissions. Fresh reviews, recorded patches and declared checks provide evidence for the inspected revision, not provider attestation or a proof of correctness. Source application is explicit, checks freshness and patch integrity, and retains uncertain application intent for recovery. It does not commit or push changes. Host services, unrelated writers and provider billing remain outside these boundaries.

docs.title: Validation gates
docs.text:
make test-sandbox exercises real broker/worker isolation, destination policy, disk caps and dynamic teams. make test-research uses isolated command actors to verify game accounting and continuation without provider calls. make test-soak checks bounded execution, restarts and one in-flight crash. CI runs these in a separate sandbox job whose namespace preflight must pass; unavailable isolation fails that job instead of silently omitting coverage.

Reproducible workflow checks and provider opt-ins are described in workflow validation. Managed isolation checks do not establish that a separately configured workflow or provider will run correctly.

make test-resources verifies actual cgroup controls on a suitable Linux host. Provider-native calls, SSH placement, multi-day operation and statistically powered behavioral studies need their own recorded runs. A green command-only suite does not establish those outcomes. Use the provider compatibility guide to check a selected integration, and the study guide to plan measurements and report limitations.

docs.title: Evaluating broader claims
docs.text: Comparative task quality needs matched single-agent and team baselines with independent artifact checks. Behavioral claims need validated extraction, counterbalanced actor/model assignments, justified sample sizes and independent scoring. Large-scale operation needs concurrent native worker measurements; logical broker clients are a different workload. Long-running reliability needs wall-clock observation under realistic provider interruptions, credential refresh and storage growth. These claims remain open until those measurements exist.

docs.title: Folders, terminal panes and reattachment
docs.text: amx is the Agentmux command. Workspaces contain registered agent sessions; each session has a stable ID, project directory and native process. A tmux window can show one agent, several agents, or ordinary scratch shells.

docs.title: Navigate the dashboard
docs.text:
Tab or Shift+Tab switches focus between the session sidebar and the current view's content. The purple header says where Up/Down acts.

Focus Up/Down Enter Sessions sidebar Select another agent Open its native terminal Board Select a message Read the full message Connections / Links Select a recipient; sidebar selects the sender Open the selected sender's native terminal Memory Select a namespace or entry Open entries or read the selected entry Tasks Select a task Read the task and its result Existing terminals Select an observed terminal Show its original terminal details Teams Select a consented team Read the team details Events Select and pin an event Read the event details

Left/Right and 1–8 change views. Ctrl+P searches sessions from anywhere: Enter opens the native terminal, Tab selects it in the workbench, and Esc cancels. Ctrl+K opens searchable Actions. Esc closes an editor, reader or namespace first; from ordinary content it focuses the sidebar. F1 returns from a native terminal to your dashboard.

In Connections, press [ to focus SENDER or ] to focus RECIPIENT, then Up/Down to choose that identity. Tab and Shift+Tab also switch between them. Only the focused label shows the arrow hint and purple highlight. Focus changes preserve both selected identities and permissions; Left/Right continues to change views.

docs.title: Choose a session's folder
docs.text:
Start the default Claude/Codex pair in a project:

amx up -s daily -p ~/projects/api

Add agents in the same or another project:

amx new review --harness codex -p ~/projects/api -s daily
amx new notes --harness claude -p ~/projects/research -s daily
amx a review -s daily

-p is short for --project. It must name an existing directory. Without -p, up and new use the shell's current directory. One workspace can contain agents from unrelated projects; sharing a workspace grants no peer communication or shared-memory access by itself.

In the dashboard, Shift+N inherits the selected session's provider and project. Its final review shows both, plus the provider-default model and trusted local host execution; it does not copy an existing model override or sandbox. Ctrl+O while entering the optional title opens advanced settings, including the project directory. Cancelling the review starts no provider. A running conversation's project is not changed by relabeling it: add a new session when you want a different project.

docs.title: Use normal scratch shells and windows
docs.text:
Press Ctrl-b, release both keys, then press the final key:

Keys Result Ctrl-b % Shell beside the current pane Ctrl-b " Shell below the current pane Ctrl-b arrow Focus another pane Ctrl-b z Zoom/unzoom the current pane Ctrl-b c New scratch window Ctrl-b ! Move the current pane into its own window Ctrl-b w Choose a workspace window Ctrl-b n / p Next/previous window Ctrl-b d Detach; keep the workspace running

New shells/windows inherit the selected agent's project. From a scratch shell, they inherit that shell's current directory, including a later cd. Scratch windows and the normal breakout key are anchored to the workspace, so disposing an attachment does not kill them. They appear again on reattachment.

Scratch shells run on the host. Splitting beside a sandboxed agent does not create another sandbox. Starting claude or codex manually in such a shell creates an ordinary external native session. It can appear in Existing terminals where recognized, but it does not inherit the neighboring agent's identity, role or permissions. Use amx new to create a registered session, or amx connect OBSERVED_ID and the printed manual setup to coordinate an existing conversation.

docs.title: Put multiple agents in one tmux window
docs.text:
For two already-running registered sessions:

amx split claude review -s daily
amx split claude review --vertical -s daily

The first ID is the destination; the second terminal moves beside it. The default is side by side; --vertical stacks panes. If they already share a window, the command focuses the second terminal without moving it again. The status label lists the agent IDs, and pane borders identify each agent. Their processes, conversations and coordination permissions stay the same.

From an agent or scratch shell inside the workspace, one ID is enough:

amx split review

It moves review beside the current pane. Dashboard and runtime-service windows are excluded. To return an agent to a separate window:

amx unsplit review -s daily

For a new agent, run amx new ... first, then amx split ID using its printed ID. Agentmux does not silently launch a duplicate conversation to arrange panes.

Native windows are shared across attachments, like normal linked tmux windows. Their layout and active pane are shared too. Each attachment retains its own dashboard, drafts and selected window. Two attachments focused on different windows remain independent; two viewing the same combined window see its pane changes. Closing a native pane/window ends its affected terminal processes; use amx remove ID when you also want to revoke that registered identity.

docs.title: Reopen a work session
docs.text:
amx                  # Workbench
amx a                # Last live native terminal
amx a review -s daily # Exact registered conversation
amx ui -s daily      # Workbench explicitly

Inside an owned attachment, an omitted workspace selector uses that exact workspace. Outside, bare amx or amx a uses the sole running workspace or shows a chooser when several are running. Commands with an explicit agent ID still use workspace work outside an attachment unless you provide -s.

Press / or Ctrl+F in the startup/resume workspace chooser or the workbench's Ctrl+W picker, then type to filter by name, path or status; arrows or Ctrl+N/P select a match, Ctrl+U clears and Enter opens the exact displayed workspace. Non-interactive amx shows active workspaces first and a short saved summary; amx ws retains the full inventory. amx context [-s NAME] prints the ordinary command target and its selection source without attaching or starting agents.

The Ctrl+W picker keeps your open draft, reader or action review intact. Esc returns to that panel. Once filtering, j, k and q are literal text; use arrows or Ctrl+N/P to navigate. amx COMMAND --help gives focused everyday command guidance; amx help all is the complete reference.

amx a restores an attachment's last live agent when available, otherwise the workspace's last live selection. If none is available, it opens the workbench. It neither starts a provider nor chooses a provider-history conversation. An exited agent needs the explicit relaunch flow, such as amx relaunch review --resume picker -s daily.

Installing a newer amx does not restart live agents. Reattach with the newer command for the updated dashboard and attachment controls. A native window manually moved to an unrelated tmux server/session is outside the tracked workspace; use amx split / amx unsplit for registered agent layouts.

docs.title: Trace coverage and operational recovery
docs.text:
For current reporting, start with amx observe --session work, then inspect the printed exact task with amx task TASK_ID --open --session work. The observability guide separates worker check-ins, native event observations, adapter readiness and retained outcomes. These controls are included in v0.15.0. Live progress contains metadata only; opt-in traces below contain sensitive prepared input and adapter events.

agents:
  coder:
    trace:
      enabled: true
      max_turn_bytes: 33554432
      max_total_bytes: 268435456

Opt-in local traces contain the exact prepared owner role/task/observations, adapter-visible native JSON events and final result/usage. Known credential values are redacted before writing. Traces can still contain sensitive task, code and tool content; files are private and never mounted into agent sandboxes.

Each turn is a JSONL HMAC chain using a private controller key. A terminal marker and task-completion anchor bind the sequence and byte count. The broker verifies the trace before accepting a traced task completion. Capacity is reserved before claim; hitting the turn limit stops the native process and records failure rather than silently dropping evidence. Keep an owner's copy of task anchors outside the state directory if independent later comparison is needed. Someone holding the owner key and editable database can rewrite both; this is authenticated local evidence, not public immutable attestation.

amx managed trace list --state STATE --agent coder
amx managed trace verify --state STATE --agent coder --id TRACE_ID --mac TASK_MAC
amx managed trace show --state STATE --agent coder --id TRACE_ID

These commands require the state owner's credential/filesystem access and work with the broker offline. They reject malformed framing, altered records, truncation, data after the footer and mismatched anchors. Signed record envelopes require the nine canonical fields exactly once; duplicate fields and case aliases are rejected before authentication. Native event data remains covered by its record's MAC. show authenticates a private capture before emitting those exact captured JSONL bytes, so a concurrent append or replacement cannot add unverified content to the output. Copy traces together with their task anchors to owner-controlled archive storage before intentionally freeing capacity; never delete active turn files.

docs.title: Portable authenticated bundles
docs.text:
An owner can export a completed trace as a private signed bundle. Export first checks the exact captured JSONL against the local HMAC chain and optional task anchor, then signs that content, its SHA256, session, agent, coverage and summary with an Ed25519 owner-exporter key. The key is created once at STATE/traces/portable-signing.key with mode 0600 and is never included in a bundle. Neither the HMAC key nor broker credentials or environment snapshots are exported. The bundle contains the trace's task/tool content, so it remains sensitive even when known credential values were redacted during capture.

amx managed trace export --state STATE --agent coder --id TRACE_ID \
  --mac TASK_MAC --output /private/trace-bundle.json
# Copy the printed fingerprint through an independently trusted channel.
# Verification works on another machine with no state directory or secret key:
amx managed trace verify-bundle --input /private/trace-bundle.json \
  --trust OWNER_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256

The trust fingerprint is mandatory: an embedded public key alone does not establish who exported a file. Verification authenticates the pinned owner exporter's signed attestation of local verification, not a model provider, unmodifiable execution environment, or the truth of agent output. An owner with the signing key can issue another bundle. Retain the fingerprint outside the state directory, protect/back up the signing key, and compare task anchors independently when that stronger comparison matters. Bundle creation refuses an existing output path; captured input to an export is bounded to 64 MiB and the encoded bundle to 128 MiB. Verification never extracts or executes files. Offline verification does not contact providers or read local broker state.
